# editor’s introduction

**W** **hen Jonathan Edwards lent to his fifteen-year-old son Timothy, a student at the College of New Jersey in Princeton, a stack of eleven books in spring 1754, one of the volumes offered this adage: “There are few, if any Books, out of which a Man of Learning may not extract something for his use.”** **1** **The advice was apt, for it had appeared in the** **Guardian,** **a British periodical issued in 1713 by Sir Richard Steele and Joseph Addison that mixed observations on religion and morality with less edifying fare, such as a mock want ad for a missing “Modesty-Piece” (a garment covering a lady’s bosom).** **2** **By now the** **Guardian** **’s political origin in the Whig opposition to Tory foreign policy had been obscured by the passing of four decades, yet the popularity of bound sets of this short-lived periodical was such that twenty-six editions would appear by the end of the eighteenth century.** **3** **Urbane wit, it seems, had a long shelf life, even in the household of a sober clergyman on the periphery of Britain’s empire.**

**1.** **The Guardian** **(London, 1714), no. 148, p. 236; critical edition by John Calhoun Stephens (Lexington, Univ. Press of Kentucky, 1982), 483.**

The present volume, the final installment of **The Works of Jonathan Edwards,**is about Edwards’ world of books. In many ways, this world is alien to the typical reader today. A number of the important writers Edwards mentions or uses—Laurence Echard, Benjamin Hoadly, Nathaniel Lardner, Thomas Manton, John Oldmixon, and William Whiston, to name a few—are now largely forgotten. Edwards also read about certain subjects that modern Americans would find strange, such as the political threat posed by Jacobites or the medicinal use of water infused with tar. Yet in other respects, Edwards’ book world is oddly familiar. The many works he read on natural religion—the knowledge of God attained through reason rather than revelation—resemble the current industry of publications on science and religion. And just as advice and how-to books are reliable bestsellers today, a three-volume advice book on relationships

and religion, **The Ladies Library**(1714), was the work Edwards lent to his acquaintances most frequently; he also sent it back with Timothy to college. Any attempt to reconstruct Edwards’ book world, and therefore to understand his conceptual horizons, must reckon with both the familiar and the strange in his reading.

**In painting a picture of Edwards’ bibliographical universe, this volume relies principally on two heretofore unpublished documents: his “Catalogue” (a record of book interests, especially books he hoped to acquire) and his “Account Book” (in part a record of books he lent to family, parishioners, and fellow clergy). Long ago, Edwards’ biographer Ola Winslow concluded that the “Catalogue” was “in many ways the most interesting of all his manuscript remains.”** **4** **Yet its 720 entries, many of them cryptic and containing multiple book references, presented formidable challenges for scholars, especially when library searches still had to be conducted using card catalogues. Now, with the advent of online databases linking libraries worldwide, reliable annotation of the “Catalogue,” along with the more recently discovered “Account Book,” has become possible in a way unimaginable to earlier generations of scholars.** **5**

Until now, the only published attempt to comprehend JE’s book interests over his whole career was Thomas H. Johnson, “Jonathan Edwards’ Background of Reading,” **Publications of the Colonial Society of Massachusetts**28 (1931), 193–222. Johnson, who did not have access to the “Account Book,” surveyed the books listed in the “Catalogue,” comparing them with citations and quotations of authors in JE’s major treatises. Johnson’s article appeared simultaneously with an unpublished thesis, James Stillman Caskey, “Jonathan Edwards’ ‘Catalogue’” (B.D. thesis, Chicago Theological Seminary, 1931), which attempted an initial transcript and annotation of the “Catalogue.” Caskey’s work later informed William Sparkes Morris’ 1956 University of Chicago Ph.D. dissertation, posthumously published as **The Young Jonathan Edwards: A Reconstruction**(Brooklyn, Carlson Publishing, 1991; repr. Ironically, both the English Enlightenment and the Reformed tradition, though seemingly polar opposites, partook of a sixteenth-century Protestant iconoclasm that placed the book over the church and its sacraments as the principal source of religious authenticity and authority. For

**political, social, and intellectual milieu of Edwards and his circle, showing us how British these colonials were (or at least aspired to be) and how thoroughly their outlook depended on developments across the Atlantic. Most important, the documents in this volume enable us to track Edwards’ reading at every stage of his career, affording us the most comprehensive view yet of his own intellectual evolution. The resulting picture revises the assumption, inherited from Thomas H. Johnson’s early study, that though Edwards read more widely than most of his contemporaries, his intellectual world was still “tightly bound by theological dogma.”** **7** **To be sure, Edwards was firmly grounded in the Reformed scholasticism of his forebears. Like his father and grandfather, he read what Cotton Mather called the “Good old Puritan Divinity,” which shared with the high Protestant orthodoxy of continental Europe a sophisticated technical vocabulary grounded in classical and medieval thought. But unlike ministers of earlier generations in New England, Edwards came of age at a time when a new style of literature—variously termed by its contemporaries “polite,” “catholick,” or “latitudinarian”—was coming into vogue. This was the literature of the “republic of letters” (another eighteenth-century concept, to be explored more fully below), which historians now recognize as a vanguard of the Enlightenment. Edwards’ book lists reveal more vividly than ever before how profoundly this culture of Enlightenment letters set his intellectual agenda, serving alternately as a foil and a model for his own literary production. Indeed, the fruitful tension between Enlightenment “latitude” and Reformed traditionalism animated Edwards’ entire career, immersing him in a culture that was increasingly dispassionate toward old orthodoxies even as he remained firmly rooted in a religious system that presupposed the existence of only one truth.** **8**

Both groups regarded reading as a powerful antidote to medieval “superstition.” Edwards’ world was therefore a culture of the book to its core. In the pages to follow, we shall see the many genres in which this book culture was manifest. The term “book,” moreover, will be used to encompass not only leather-bound volumes such as the Bible but also the more ephemeral materials—newspapers, individual sermons and tracts—that were part of Edwards’ reading.** **9**

**As Wilson Kimnach has noted, the two earliest and most important influences on Edwards as a thinker were the Bible and the preaching of his father, Timothy, which together provided the idiom and rhetorical conventions for much of his later writing.** **1** **The Bible’s influence, in particular, should not be underestimated: the Edwards of Perry Miller’s celebrated 1949 biography, who seems to prefer John Locke to Scripture, is a misrepresentation.** **2** **In his posthumously published “Personal Narrative,” Edwards attested that throughout his life he had “the greatest delight in the holy Scriptures, of any book whatsoever,” and his exegetical writings reveal that in many respects, he inherited the essentially precritical scripturalism of his Puritan forebears.** **3**

In contrast to Timothy’s collection, Stoddard’s library contained more philosophical and even medieval scholastic texts. Stoddard, who preceded Timothy as a student at Harvard by two decades, made an inventory

**training for a ministerial vocation. Candidates for admission to the Collegiate School (later renamed Yale) had to be conversant in Latin, and by age seven Edwards was already learning this language from his father and older sisters. Timothy also gave his children writing assignments and probably instruction in elementary arithmetic. Little else is known about Edwards’ early education beyond what can be inferred about the family atmosphere, which, despite its conventional piety, also presented young Jonathan with the possibility of departing from tradition. His grandfather Solomon Stoddard, whom he would eventually succeed as pastor in Northampton, Massachusetts, had run afoul of Boston traditionalists like Increase Mather for liberalizing strict standards of admission to the Lord’s Supper while also arguing for greater clerical authority. Timothy Edwards, who advocated his father-in-law’s clericalism but not his open communion, encountered significant resistance from his East Windsor, Connecticut, congregation. Conversations over this protracted conflict would have been frequent at home during Jonathan’s childhood.** **4**

Not surprisingly, Timothy’s library contained controversial books by Stoddard on the Lord’s Supper, along with volumes on a variety of other doctrinal questions. Two inventories of Timothy’s books (included in this volume) are heavy on Puritan titles, including works by such seventeenth-century Nonconformists as Richard Baxter, John Goodwin, John Flavel, John Owen, and William Twisse. The family’s library also included sermons and treatises by such New Englanders as Thomas Hooker, Increase Mather, Cotton Mather, John Norton, Ebenezer Pemberton, Sr., Joseph Sewall, Samuel Willard, and William Williams. The presence of such New England figures as the Mathers, especially on old Puritan questions of “practical divinity” (the branch of theology related to the Christian life), is notably stronger in Timothy’s library than in Jonathan’s later reading—an important generational difference. Last, among the relatively few nontheological books that Jonathan probably encountered in his father’s library were a handful of classical texts (Cicero, Ovid, Virgil); a few grammars, lexicons, and almanacs; and a copy of the Connecticut charter.

**In the meantime, Edwards, who was not quite thirteen years old, entered Yale College in autumn 1716. The infant institution was at the time torn by a controversy over its permanent location, and Edwards spent the first three years with the faction temporarily settled at Wethersfield (ten miles from his home in East Windsor), which was led by his cousin Elisha Williams. Logic was the first subject in the Yale curriculum, and the Harvard-trained Williams, as Norman Fiering has shown, was an exponent of the Port-Royal logic of Antoine Arnauld and Pierre Nicole, authors of** **La Logique, ou L’Art de penser** **(1662), which rejected Aristotelian categories, or what Williams called “rote names of arbitrary signification.” This influential text of Cartesian logic was still being consulted in English translation in Edwards’ senior year, and a copy with his signature survives in Yale’s Beinecke Library.** **7** **Arnauld and Nicole were part of a longer tradition of logic, beginning with the sixteenth-century French humanist Petrus Ramus, that also included the seventeenth-century Dutch logicians Burgersdijck and Heereboord, whom Stoddard had**

**Unfortunately, no direct evidence of the overall curriculum at Wethersfield survives, but records of Harvard’s regimen, along with other documents, testify to Edwards’ likely course of study.** **1** **In addition to studying logic, he continued to refine his Latin and Greek and also took up Hebrew.** **2** **Rhetoric was another essential subject, probably covered through William Dugard’s** **Rhetorices Elementa** **(1648). In the fields of metaphysics and ethics, the Cambridge Platonist Henry More was then the standard, along with Heereboord and possibly others. More (1614– 87), according to Fiering, was probably the most influential philosopher in America during Edwards’ college days. More’s** **Enchiridion Ethicum** **(1667) and** **Enchiridion Metaphysicum** **(1671) were often summarized in Harvard student notebooks, though the widespread use of his works in New England was ironic given his rejection of Calvinist orthodoxy in favor of a more benevolent view of both God and humans.** **3** **Meanwhile, in science and mathematics Edwards probably studied Jacques Rohault’s Cartesian physics in the 1697 Latin translation (with Newtonian annotations) by Samuel Clarke (see “Catalogue,” no. 70). ### The Dummer Books at Yale

**Finally there was divinity. Yale students, like their Harvard counterparts, participated in regular disputations on the principal loci. Early American Puritans had typically studied Calvinism as refracted through William Ames’** **Medulla Sacrae Theologiae** **(1627; English translation,** **The Marrow of Sacred Divinity,** **1642), and Edwards undoubtedly was exposed to this text; the Yale Library owns a copy used by his college roommate and cousin Elisha Mix. Ames was eventually superseded, at Harvard at least, by the** **Compendium Theologiae Christianae** **(1626; English translation,** **The Abridgment of Christian Divinitie,** **1650) of the Swiss Calvinist Johannes Wollebius. Another widely circulating Continental systematic theology was Peter van Mastricht’s** **Theoretico-Practica Theologia** **(1699), a work that would later loom large as a source for Edwards.** **6**

**Weighty tomes by Reformed systematicians, however, were about to be joined at Yale by more polite fare, thanks to the donation of a major book collection from London. These books brought an infusion of recent intellectual currents, most notably Latitudinarianism, the dominant outlook in the Church of England since the Restoration, which emphasized moderation and tolerance as antidotes to the partisan strife that had so long characterized English religious life. Anticipated by the Cambridge Platonists Ralph Cudworth and Henry More, the Latitudinarians avoided both Puritan and high-church extremes, espousing instead a broad, establishment faith based on Christianity’s “essentials,” chiefly its moral teachings. Latitudinarianism tended toward an Arminian confidence in human ability and also entailed a strong interest in natural religion, or the knowledge of God revealed through nature and human reason.** **7** **By the late seventeenth century, prominent Latitudinarians in**

**But Latitudinarian ideas, though well worn in London—and even in Boston** **1** **—by the early eighteenth century, were still avoided at Yale until Jeremiah Dummer, London agent for the Massachusetts and Connecticut colonies, gave the college more than eight hundred books covering every major branch of learning.** **2** **Though the books were donated in 1714, they were not accessible until Edwards’ senior year, by which**

**the Anglican hierarchy included not only the bishop of Worcester, Edward Stillingfleet, but also the archbishop of Canterbury, John Tillotson, whose sermons remained wildly popular decades after his death in 1694. Among Tillotson’s admirers was John Locke, whose** **Reasonableness of Christianity** **(1695) also revealed a Latitudinarian temper. Later figures friendly to the Latitudinarian perspective included the Anglican bishop Benjamin Hoadly, the philosopher Samuel Clarke, and the politicians and essayists Joseph Addison, Richard Steele, and Anthony Ashley Cooper, third earl of Shaftesbury.** **8** **By the early eighteenth century the polite, Latitudinarian style was so pervasive in the Church of England that the once-triumphant Calvinism of the Puritan revolution had virtually disappeared as an effective force in English life.** **9**

**By themselves, of course, the volumes posed no threat to Congregational orthodoxy, but as Edmund S. Morgan once quipped, the “trouble with books is that people** **will** **read them.”** **5** **Rumors about the nature of the Dummer gift soon spread beyond New Haven, such that one New Jersey pastor whose son was a Yale student wrote to Cotton Mather in 1722 that he was “frighted” by reports of “Arminian Books . . . cryed up in Yale Colledge for Eloquence & Learning.”** **6** **The danger of the Dum-mer books was made starkly apparent later that year when Yale rector Timothy Cutler, former tutor Samuel Johnson, and five other local ministers declared their Congregational ordinations invalid and announced their intention of seeking Episcopal reordination. This defection to Anglicanism, as one historian has noted, had an effect similar to that which might have been produced in the twentieth century if the entire Yale football team had suddenly joined the Communist Party.** **7** **The** **Boston**

Word of the apostasy undoubtedly soon reached Edwards, who by then had completed his M.A. studies and begun a position as an unordained pastor of an English Presbyterian congregation in New York City. The diverse colony of New York had for some time been the focus of Anglican efforts to achieve a robust Church of England establishment in the northern colonies. Many New Englanders now feared that the apostasy in New Haven, along with the settlement in nearby Stratford of Anglican

**News-Letter** **reported that Yale College, which had been “set up . . . according to Scripture Rule, Free of Humane Traditions and Impositions . . . is now become Corrupt.” The aging Increase Mather, holding forth at Boston’s Old North Church, bewailed the “Connecticut Apostacie,” and within a year the shock of creeping infidelity contributed largely to his death, according to his son Cotton and the poet Edward Taylor, who opined that “Cutler’s Cutlary gave th’killing Stob.”** **8**

Anglicanism had long been New England’s bugbear because it accommodated Arminianism (which violated the Calvinist doctrine of God’s sovereignty) and embraced episcopacy (which violated the Puritan belief that the office of bishop was unscriptural).

**The major reason cited by most observers, and the apostates themselves, for the Episcopal defection was the influence of the Dummer collection, with its substantial number of Arminian and Latitudinarian titles. Cutler and his co-conspirators had been meeting regularly in his home to discuss the books—such fateful treatises as Bishop Hoadly’s** **Reasonableness of Conformity to the Church of England** **(1703)** **9** **—and had concluded that Congregational polity was fatally flawed and violated the biblical model of church government. Out of these discussions came the group’s dramatic apostasy, carefully timed for Yale’s commencement on September 12, 1722. The Yale trustees, convened by Connecticut governor Gurdon Saltonstall, immediately dismissed Cutler and voted to require of future rectors and tutors evidence of “opposition to Armenian & prelatical Corruptions.” Meanwhile Dummer himself bristled at the “slander” that his books had been the source of all the trouble, insisting that “there never was an Eminent Dissenter . . . whose works are not in that Collection.”** **1**

### The Beginning and Nature of the “Catalogue”

It was within this political context that Edwards began keeping his book wish list.**

3. Marsden, **Jonathan Edwards,**86.

Sometime during his New York pastorate, probably in late 1722, the nineteen-year-old Edwards began keeping a catalogue of his own. Unlike Johnson’s list, Edwards’ “Catalogue” appears to have been an ongoing record of his reading priorities and interests rather than a tally of books he actually read. Though he did in fact read many of the books listed, the mere inclusion of a title in the “Catalogue” proves only that he was aware of a particular book, not that he owned it or had read it. Only when Edwards cites information from a book can we be sure he had obtained it. Thus, a distinction will be made here between books Edwards simply **lists**(or mentions in some way) and books he actually **cites.**

**The idea of a catalogue of books would not have been foreign to Edwards. The eighteenth-century British Empire was awash in printed book lists: estate inventories of the gentry’s libraries, catalogues of the wares of individual booksellers, and consolidated catalogues of multiple printers’ lists. The last-named genre had been pioneered in the late seventeenth century by the London bookseller Robert Clavell, whose quarterly** **Catalogue of Books Printed in England** **ran for four decades, until his death in 1711.** **4** **By the early eighteenth century it was not uncommon for English scholars and persons of leisure to keep a private manuscript catalogue of reading interests. Such was the case with the former Yale tutor Samuel Johnson, whose own “Catalogue,” begun in 1719 (three years before his Anglican apostasy), was a running list of books he had actually read. Between 1722 and 1752 he averaged about a book a week.** **5**

Edwards recorded the first “Catalogue” entries on single quarto leaves.

**The earliest entries of the “Catalogue” (nos. 183 and following) make clear the private nature of this manuscript. Unlike Edwards’ “Miscellanies,” which had a polished, quasi-public character, the entries here are working notations, often with greatly abbreviated author and title information, of books Edwards hoped to purchase or at least consult.** **8** **Though the cross-references give the manuscript’s later pages a more systematic quality, the private, wish-list character is apparent throughout. Early on, for example, in no. 218 (circa 1723), he lists** **De veritate religionis Christianae** **by the Dutch Remonstrant (Arminian) theologian Hugo Grotius. Edwards specifically mentions the Latitudinarian bishop Simon Patrick’s English translation of Grotius, which included an anti-Romanist discourse by Patrick at the end. But Edwards adds, in words that are crossed out: “if they are not to be Gotten together only his translation.”** **9**

**Later he stitched in quires (double leaves, folded) to make a manuscript notebook, which he bound in heavy brown paper and labeled simply “catalogue.” He wrote on both sides of each page, numbering the pages on the top outside corner. As he was commencing his Yale tutorship in 1724, he also began jotting entries on a separate letter leaf, which he never sewed into the “Catalogue” notebook. He probably began these letter-leaf entries as he was writing page 2 of the main manuscript, but since the precise chronological parallels between entries are difficult to determine, the entries are numbered here beginning with those of the letter leaf (nos. 1–182) followed by those of the manuscript proper (nos. 183–720).** **6** **Because the entries on the letter leaf and the first two manuscript pages are generally brief and written in small handwriting, Edwards was able to squeeze 296 entries—41 percent of the “Catalogue”— into this portion alone. His later entries, written in two columns, became longer as he copied advertisements for books and often quoted other authors’ bibliographical recommendations. He also began cross-referencing certain entries, using his own system of page and column numbers, and striking through many entries with a vertical line, probably indicating he had read the book referenced, though in numerous cases this cannot be proven.** **7**

The dating of the early entries is based on the ink and paper analysis of Thomas A. Schafer. See the explanation and dating tables in “Note on the Manuscripts,” below.

On the problem of JE’s strikethroughs, see “Note on the Manuscripts,” below.

JE later obtained a different translation of Grotius; see **The Works of Jonathan Edwards, 20, The “Miscellanies,” 833–1152,**ed. Amy Plantinga Pauw (New Haven, Yale Univ. Press, 2002), 240**n**1.

The private nature of the “Catalogue” is further apparent in the diversity of books Edwards lists from the beginning. This is not a roster of unimpeachable Calvinist classics, compiled for the edification of others. To be sure, many Calvinist works appear here, and a weighty Reformed dogmatic text—Mastricht’s **Theoretico-Practica Theologia**—is the main manuscript’s first entry. But Mastricht is soon followed on page 1 by listings of a number of leading Latitudinarians or their political allies: Bishop Benjamin Hoadly (no. 186); Richard Steele (no. 192); Archbishop John Tillotson (no. 206); Bishop Gilbert Burnet (nos. 211, 212);

Similar notations prioritizing his book preferences are scattered elsewhere. In no. 205, Edwards lists William Jameson’s apology for presbyterian church government, **The Sum of the Episcopal Controversy.**But in no. 221, he lists another work on church government, this one by the future lord chancellor of England, Peter King. Edwards later returned to the entry on King’s book and inserted this note in small letters: “if this be Got mr Jamesons may be Left out.”

**Edwards also listed some titles more than once, indicating his ongoing desire to obtain certain books. Early on he twice lists Milton’s** **Paradise Lost** **(nos. 20, 225), a work that was only then gaining canonical status in America.** **1** **Similarly, he twice lists Johann Arndt’s** **True Christianity** **(nos. 7, 184) and Joseph Addison’s** **Freeholder** **(nos. 25, 243), and three times lists Herman Moll’s** **Atlas Geographus** **(nos. 145, 185, 250). In some cases, the last mention of a book indicates that Edwards had finally obtained it. Thus, he lists Richard Baxter’s** **Practical Works** **twice (nos. 134, 297) before quoting a book recommendation from it in no. 349. Similarly, he lists the Presbyterian Robert Fleming’s** **Fulfilling of the Scripture** **(1669) four times over almost two decades: twice around 1724 (nos. 60, 278); a third time around 1731 (no. 340), when he cites the Church of Scotland minister Thomas Halyburton’s recommendation of the book; and a fourth time around 1742 (no. 442), when he cites an advertisement for the fifth corrected edition of Fleming’s text. Edwards finally obtained Fleming soon thereafter, for he cites the fifth edition two times in** **Some Thoughts Concerning the Present Revival** **(issued in 1743).** **2**

Much later, in no. 690 (from 1755 or 1756), JE quotes a line from Milton secondhand from the Anglican poet James Hervey. Seventeenth-century American colonists had been more likely to read Milton’s controversial and prose works than **Paradise Lost**(1667), which gained considerable popularity only in the eighteenth century. See Louis B. Wright, **The Cultural Life of the American Colonies, 1607–1763**(New York, Harper and Row, 1957), 143; cf. Miller, **The New England Mind: The Seventeenth Century,**91.

**Edwards’ interest in natural religion went hand in hand with his lifelong pursuit of clues to God’s cosmic plan in world affairs. Consequently, he evinced an early fascination with history and non-Protestant religions, as a brief list penned in the upper right-hand corner of page 1 reveals. Under the heading “Books to be enquired for,” he lists several broad subject areas (nos. 229–39), including “the best Geography,” “the best history of the world,” “the best exposition of the Apoca[lypse]” (the book of Revelation), “[those] Which are the most usefull & necessary of the Fathers,” “the best Chronology,” “the best historical Dictionary of the Nature of Bayle’s Dictionary,” and even “the best that treats of the Cabbalistical learning of the Jews.” Edwards’ curiosity about Kabbalah (reiterated in no. 253) perhaps resulted from his interaction with a Jewish neighbor in New York City, a man he later described in** **Religious Affections** **as “the devoutest person that ever I saw in my life.”** **4** **This personal contact may also have intensified Edwards’ early interest in the Talmud (no. 264), Philo (no. 267), and Maimonides (no. 268). Similarly, he sought “a book Comparing all Religions with the Xtian” (no. 261), foreshadowing his dogged quest later in life for independent confirmation**

**Bishop Simon Patrick (no. 218, in the aforementioned entry on Grotius); John Locke (no. 219); Shaftesbury (no. 220); and Daniel Finch, the second earl of Nottingham (no. 223). Edwards also lists on the first page two important periodicals, Addison and Steele’s** **Guardian** **(no. 191) and John Trenchard and Thomas Gordon’s** **Independent Whig** **(no. 210), as well as the twin conduct books,** **The Ladies Library** **and** **The Gentleman’s Library** **(no. 208). Along with these Latitudinarian and polite works, several key titles on science and natural religion appear: Isaac Newton’s** **Principia** **and** **Opticks** **(no. 194), the Dutch mathematician Bernard Nieuwentijt’s** **Religious Philosopher** **(no. 196),** **3** **and the Anglican scientist and theologian William Whiston’s** **Astronomical Principles of Religion** **(no. 216) and** **New Theory of the Earth** **(no. 224).**

**Arminianism was therefore on Edwards’ mind when Yale, with its Dummer collection still beckoning in the library, offered him a position as tutor in May 1724. Though he had served at Bolton barely six months, he left the post within two weeks of Yale’s offer. Not long after his arrival in New Haven in June, he apparently spent several weeks in the library browsing through books and recording titles on the letter leaf (an envelope addressed to him by his father).** **8** **The first entry on this separate leaf—simply “Bible”—has an almost talismanic quality, testifying again to his obeisance to the Puritan principle that Scripture must be the judge of all things. Many of the following entries, moreover, show his allegiance to the Puritan tradition’s anti-Arminianism. We find here works by such Calvinists (or honorary Calvinists) as Elisha Coles (no. 12), John Flavel**

**of key Christian doctrines, from the Trinity to the immortality of the soul, in pre-Christian and non-Christian sources.** **5**

**Edwards’ stint in the relatively cosmopolitan port of New York would prove brief. Around the time he was jotting “Books to be enquired for,” his father was maneuvering to bring him back into his own orbit by securing for Jonathan a call to the parish in Bolton, Connecticut, just fifteen miles from the family home in East Windsor. Though he was reluctant to leave New York, Jonathan dutifully agreed, first moving back to East Windsor to prepare his master’s degree** **Quaestio,** **which he successfully defended in New Haven in September 1723 before assuming his Bolton duties in November.** **6** **Signficantly, the** **Quaestio,** **composed less than a year after the fateful Connecticut Apostasy, confuted Arminianism by reasserting—in Latin—a Reformation axiom: “A sinner is not justified in the sight of God, except through the righteousness of Christ obtained by faith.” Because the Arminians make justification conditional upon human obedience, Edwards argued, they in effect make the sinner his own redeemer. To this notion, he opposed the doctrines of free grace and absolute divine sovereignty, which became recurring themes in his early sermons.** **7**

**The letter-leaf entries also reveal the continuing political and religious fallout from the Connecticut Apostasy. A cryptic, crossed-out notation, “to the Deists and Jews” (no. 18a), is probably a reference to** **A Short and Easy Method with the Deists,** **which was often printed with a second part against the Jews.** **9** **These apologies for Trinitarian orthodoxy are less important than their author, the Irish Anglican priest Charles Leslie (1650–1722), a leading Jacobite and nonjuror, or one who refused to swear loyalty to William and Mary after the overthrow of England’s last Catholic king, James II, in the Glorious Revolution of 1688. Leslie, who after the revolution had served as Protestant chaplain to James’ exiled court in France, had been one of the most zealous Jacobite apologists for a hereditary royal succession,** **1** **the divine right of kings, and the direct appointment of bishops by the anointed monarch.** **2** **He became notorious in New England after John Checkley, an Anglican convert and Jacobite, reprinted Leslie’s** **Short and Easy Method** **in Boston in 1719 and again in 1723, the second time appending to it his own pro-Anglican** **Discourse Concerning Episcopacy,** **for which Checkley was convicted of seditious libel and fined fifty pounds by the Massachusetts General Court. Checkley, who had already enraged the Boston establishment for other attacks on its theology and polity, was soon blamed for the Connecticut Apostasy, which many New Englanders came to regard as part of an ongoing Jacobite conspiracy to overthrow the House of Hanover, inaugurated with the accession of George I in 1714.** **3**

When James Francis Edward, son of James II, was born in June 1688, he took precedence over his Protestant half-sisters Mary and Anne in the Stuart succession. Fearing another Catholic king, a group of influential English politicians encouraged Mary’s husband, William of Orange (a Dutch Calvinist), to invade and overthrow James II. The Jacobites viewed William’s action as an illegitimate usurpation of the rightful succession.

The Bill of Rights (1689) effectively transferred sovereignty from Crown to Parliament. Leslie insisted that civil government by monarchs and church government by bishops had been instituted by God and that the two protected and reinforced each other. See Robert D. Cornwall, “Charles Leslie,” in **ODNB;**and Ronald N. Stromberg, **Religious Liberalism in Eighteenth-Century England**(Oxford, Oxford Univ. Press, 1954), 126–27.

### The Republic of Letters: Sources of Book References

**This political context helps explain a series of enigmatic entries written on the other side of the “Catalogue” letter leaf in the upper right-hand corner. The notations “Against Captain kelly” (no. 175), “penalties Commons Against Roches[ter]” (no. 176), “Bp. of Rochester a double Guard” (no. 178), and “Dr friend Committed to tower” (no. 181; cf. no. 180) are all references to the Atterbury Plot—an abortive Jacobite military scheme in 1722 to replace George I with the Old Pretender (the son of James II). Among the conspirators were Francis Atterbury (the bishop of Rochester), George Kelly (an agent for the exiled Stu-arts), and John Freind (a physician and chemist). All three were arrested and imprisoned in the Tower of London.** **4** **Reports on these events in the New England press undoubtedly excited Edwards’ hope that the forces of popery and prelacy were predestined for defeat in God’s good providence.** **5** **Indeed, throughout his career Edwards remained an avid observer of Jacobite and other political intrigue, for like his Puritan forebears, he believed that the fortunes of all nations were governed not by chance but by God’s immediate superintendence.**

**Edwards’ abiding interest in “signs of the times” meant that he was an indefatigable source collector. Newspapers were one important source on the progress of God’s kingdom. As Edwards later recalled in his** **Personal Narrative,** **“I used to be earnest to read public news-letters, mainly for that end; to see if I could not find some news favorable to the interest of religion in the world.”** **6** **Newspapers also provided occasional announcements of new books. Edwards learned, for example, of the six-volume history** **Magna Britannia** **from the** **Boston News-Letter,** **a weekly newspaper and the first successful American publication of its kind.** **7**

**Founded in 1704 by the Boston postmaster John Campbell and modeled after the** **London Gazette,** **the** **News-Letter** **devoted most of its space to reports reprinted verbatim from London papers. Far from being mere filler, this London news was eagerly sought by American colonists, who still considered themselves British and wanted to feel connected to the empire’s great capital.** **8**

**Edwards was no exception in his desire to escape provincial isolation. Even as he was scanning newspapers for signs of the world’s end, he was driven by worldly ambition. In a memorandum to himself written during his Yale tutorship, he revealed his aspiration to make a name for himself in the European republic of letters: “Before I venture to publish in London, to make some experiment in my own country; to play at small games first, that I may gain some experience in writing.”** **9** **In the same memorandum he cited as a literary model the genre of philosophical dialogue employed by Shaftesbury, the famous Whig moralist, who had argued for a political order based on the natural sociability and virtue of free and equal gentlemen.** **1** **Edwards was strongly attracted to Whiggish periodicals from London that embodied Shaftesbury’s gospel of sociability and politeness, an ethic its promoters billed as the antidote to Tory absolutism and high-church priestcraft. We have already seen Edwards’ interest in one such polite periodical, the** **Guardian,** **which he twice lists early in the “Catalogue” (nos. 9 and 191) and later owned. Early in the “Catalogue” he also lists the** **Guardian** **’s more celebrated predecessor, the** **Spectator** **(no. 241), as well as its sequel, the** **Englishman** **(no. 242).** **2** **In addition, he mentions Addison’s** **Freeholder** **(nos. 25 and 243), and Addison and Steele’s** **Lover** **and** **Reader** **(no. 255).**

**The second periodical source of book references for Edwards were learned journals specifically devoted to bibliographical culture. These differed from trade publications such as Robert Clavell’s** **Catalogue of Books Printed in England,** **which were little more than price lists of titles. The new learned journals not only announced new books but also offered extended reviews and excerpts, all in an effort to cultivate the life of the mind.** **5** **The first example of this genre in England was** **History of the Works of the Learned,** **founded by the nonjuror Samuel Parker and others, which ran monthly from 1699 to 1712. Edwards mentions this journal in the “Catalogue” (no. 356), though it is not clear whether he ever had access to it. He also mentions** **Memoirs of Literature** **(no. 361), edited by Michael de la Roche, a Huguenot refugee who settled in London after Louis XIV revoked the Edict of Nantes in 1685. Far more important for Edwards was** **The Present State of the Republick of Letters,** **published monthly from 1728 to 1736. Edited by Andrew Reid, about whom little is known, it billed itself as “a general view of the state of learning throughout Europe” and carried announcements and abstracts of new books on all major subjects. Edwards cites book recommendations from it sixteen times in the “Catalogue,” beginning in the early 1730s.** **6** **He was among a number of prominent colonial devotees of the journal, including Yale’s**

**As sources on politeness, these Whig dailies and thrice-weeklies were unparalleled, but for information on new books Edwards relied on two other types of periodicals.** **3** **The first was the general monthly magazine, made successful in 1731 by the journalist Edward Cave’s** **Gentleman’s Magazine.** **Besides featuring reports from Parliament and general-interest articles, these magazines also included lists of new books and occasional longer reviews. Edwards became a voracious reader of the imitator and chief rival of the** **Gentleman’s Magazine,** **the** **London Magazine,** **founded in 1732, which featured a “Monthly Catalogue” of books at the end of every issue. Edwards explicitly cites this magazine’s book recommendations sixteen times.** **4**

In their original serial form, the dailies did carry book advertisements; the **Guardian,**for example, listed some 650 separate titles (see the select list in the Stephens critical ed., pp. 591– 95). But these advertisements did not appear in the later bound editions such as that owned by JE. Comments on books in the text of the **Guardian**itself were less frequent, and JE cites only one of these (“Catalogue,” no. 226).

See nos. 390, 391, 393–404, 415, and 417.

**The new learned journals also helped give rise to the “republic of letters” as a metaphor for an ecumenical community of scholarly exchange. The term first gained currency from Pierre Bayle’s journal** **Nouvelles de la République des Lettres,** **launched in 1684. Bayle (1647–1706), another Huguenot refugee of Louis XIV’s persecution, studiously avoided religious divisiveness in his journal and urged his readers to unite behind a common pursuit of knowledge. Reciprocity and politeness thus were the cardinal rules of this imagined community, which soon spread to England, thanks to journals such as the** **Republick of Letters,** **and then on to America.** **8** **As participants in the republic of letters, Edwards and other intellectuals exchanged ideas and books, establishing not only local but also transatlantic networks.**

**Samuel Johnson and the Quaker James Logan, who served as an agent to the Penn family in Philadelphia. For these and other colonial intellectuals, periodicals such as the** **Republick of Letters** **were what Norman Fiering has called “lifeline journals,” or a means of keeping scholarly interests alive despite geographic separation from London by more than three thousand miles.** **7**

**Edwards’ earliest book exchanges were chiefly local, as when he shared volumes with other Yale students and tutors. On the “Catalogue” letter leaf, for example, he mentioned the “history of the 4 Monarchies in Mr treats study” (no. 71), evidently referring to a copy of Johannes Sleidanus’** **Key of Historie** **owned by Robert Treat, a fellow Yale tutor. Also on the letter leaf, Edwards refers to Treat’s copy of William Brattle’s** **Logick,** **a work that circulated only in manuscript until 1735. In a later “Catalogue” entry from 1737, Edwards mentions a copy of George Benson’s** **History of the First Planting of the Christian Religion** **that he saw at “Mr. diodates at new haven” (no. 388). William Diodate, a descendant of the seventeenth-century Calvinist divine Giovanni Diodati, was New Haven’s first known resident of Italian ancestry.** **9** **Whether Diodate, an avid collector of theological books, actually lent volumes to Edwards is not known, but the two men at least shared a common bibliophilism.**

See the overview by Ruth Whelan, “Republic of Letters,” in **Encyclopedia of the Enlightenment,**ed. Alan Charles Kors (New York, Oxford Univ. Press, 2003), 3:436–40. On Bayle’s influence, see also Fiering, “Transatlantic Republic of Letters,” 645–47. **His most important overseas source was the Scottish divine John Erskine, seventeen years his junior, who was influenced by Edwards’ writings and became for him a regular conduit not only of bibliographical tips but also of actual books and pamphlets. Surviving correspondence between the two men shows that between 1746 and 1757 Edwards received dozens of books from Erskine, as in 1753, when he received two packages, the first containing sixteen items and the second containing nine.** **4** **One of these books was** **Principles of Natural and Revealed Religion,** **by William Warburton, bishop of Gloucester, which Edwards quickly put to use in his “Controversies” notebook. More significant, Erskine had earlier sent him two anti-Calvinist works by the English dissenter John Taylor, who became Edwards’ chief Arminian target in** **Original Sin** **(1758).** **5** **Though the Edwards-Erskine exchanges were usually one**

**In his later career Edwards cultivated increasingly international book exchanges as he published works of his own and gained a reputation abroad. Edwards, George Whitefield, and other promoters of revival in effect established an** **evangelical** **republic of letters parallel to the broader European community of letters in which they also participated.** **1** **Edwards’ principal contacts were in Scotland, where revivals occurred in 1742 in Cambuslang (near Glasgow) and Kilsyth (near Edinburgh). In the wake of the two revivals, the Scottish Presbyterian James Robe published accounts modeled after Edwards’ own** **Faithful Narrative** **(1737) and began corresponding with Edwards soon thereafter.** **2** **Edwards also made connections with the Scottish ministers John MacLaurin, William McCulloch, and John Willison, who occasionally sent him book recommendations, as the “Catalogue” reveals.** **3**

**The growth of Edwards’ fame internationally as a revivalist brought an additional benefit for his book-collecting habits: he sometimes obtained information about new books from advertisements printed at the end of his own works. During Edwards’ lifetime his sermons and treatises appeared in print not only in Boston but also in London, Edinburgh, Glasgow, Bristol, Amsterdam, Utrecht, Magdeburg, and Leipzig.** **7** **The lack of modern copyright restrictions was partly responsible for this proliferation, and Edwards himself may never have seen the Dutch and German-language editions. But he did see the British versions, so when the second edition of his** **Faithful Narrative** **appeared in London in 1738 with two pages of book notices printed at the end, he inserted references to these advertisements in four “Catalogue” entries (nos. 378, 386, 412, and 416).**

**sided—Edwards had far less access to books on the Massachusetts frontier than Erskine enjoyed in his successive parishes near Glasgow and Ed-inburgh—Edwards did not miss an opportunity to return a favor. “I have herewith sent the two books of Mr. [Solomon] Stoddard’s you desired,” he wrote to Erskine in 1748. “The lesser of the two was my own; and though I have no other, yet you have laid me under such obligations, that I am glad I have it to send to you.”** **6** **Such were the rules of reciprocity between two gentlemen in the republic of letters.**

Two other ways in which Edwards obtained book references deserve attention. The first is that time-honored method among scholars: mining other scholars’ footnotes. Even in an age lacking the benefits of modern standards of scholarly citation, Edwards assiduously combed through books for bibliographical details—however imprecise—on other books. Sometimes this led to frustration, as when a note in the margin of **The History of Popery**(1735–36) cited simply “Spotwood’s Contin[uation] of Sleidan.” Edwards copied the citation verbatim (no. 496), perhaps never figuring out that it was probably a reference to John Spottiswood’s **History of the Church of Scotland,**a work distinct from Johannes Sleidanus’ general history of the Reformation, which had been continued by Edmund Bohun. Other books proved far more accurate and fruitful as sources of references. In a 1749 letter to Edwards, John Erskine mentioned the Anglican devotional writer James Hervey’s two-volume **Meditations and Contemplations**as “the most polite of any that has been written in an evangelical strain in this century” (no. 502). Soon thereafter, Edwards

**The final way Edwards obtained bibliographical references was from advice manuals on study, which usually included lists of recommended books. One such manual was Cotton Mather’s** **Manuductio ad Ministerium: Directions for a Candidate of the Ministry** **(1726), which Edwards obtained within two or three years of its publication. Though Mather offered counsel on practical matters ranging from nurturing the habit of daily prayer to avoiding frequent use of liquor, he devoted more than half of his volume to annotated book recommendations on every major branch of learning. With his occasionally caustic wit, Mather passed judgment on a host of works, lauding Pierre Bayle’s** **Dictionary,** **for example, as “a Work to be wondred at,” provided the reader “guard against the Manichaean Sophistry, sometimes appearing in it.”** **1** **Elsewhere he recommended a variety of texts of geography and history but could not resist lobbing a grenade at one by John Oldmixon, who had panned Mather’s own** **Magnalia Christi Americana** **nearly two decades earlier. Oldmixon’s** **British Empire in America** **was, in Mather’s view, “the most foolish and faithless Performance in this Kind, that ever Mankind was abused withal.”** **2** **Edwards evidently relished such prose, for he cited Mather’s book recommendations ten times in the “Catalogue” and probably relied on Mather’s advice in other instances not indicated.** **3** **Despite its urbane tone, Mather’s counsel was for the most part conservative and traditional,**

**obtained the book and found it a veritable storehouse of bibliographical leads, which he cited no fewer than eight times.** **8** **The following year, in a letter to Edwards, John MacLaurin mentioned that Hervey was “preparing for the publick some Composure in favor of sound doctrine” (no. 562)—evidently an advance notice of his three-volume** **Theron and Aspasio,** **a moderate Calvinist defense of the doctrine of imputed righteousness, cast in the form of a polite dialogue. Edwards procured Hervey’s new work soon after its publication in 1755 and again began mining it for citations, finding leads on at least seven books.** **9**

**Not all the advice manuals on study that Edwards used were by ministers. The manual he consulted more than any other was** **An Essay upon Study** **(1731) by the English schoolmaster and educational reformer John Clarke. Edwards first listed this title in entry no. 497, around the beginning of 1749. Within a year he had obtained a copy, for he went on to cite Clarke’s book recommendations in some twenty-one “Catalogue” entries, all from 1750.** **6** **Perhaps he was taking solace in books: the entries coincide with his final estrangement and dismissal from his Northampton congregation. A few years later, after he had settled in Stockbridge, Massachusetts, Edwards took an interest in another advice book,** **Youth’s Friendly Monitor** **(1754), by the educational reformer and later Whig political propagandist James Burgh (see no. 621). He procured a copy soon after its publication and gleaned one title—Simon Ockley’s** **History of the Saracens** **(no. 665)—from Burgh’s postscript of recommended books. Read these titles, Burgh promised, and “you will be furnished with a most noble and manly Entertainment for your leisure Hours, and may, in time, qualify yourself for the Conversation of the**

**We have seen the origins of, and sources for, the “Catalogue,” but to understand the other major documentary record of Edwards’ reading interests, the “Account Book,” it is helpful to recall the chronology of events immediately following Edwards’ tutorship. In August 1726, he received an invitation from the church at Northampton to become assistant pastor to his grandfather. Solomon Stoddard was then eighty-three, so Edwards would be poised to take over as pastor of one of New England’s most prominent parishes. Edwards resigned from Yale, arriving in Northampton in late October, and was officially ordained as assistant pastor the following February. Later that year, in July 1727, he married Sarah Pierpont, daughter of James Pierpont (the late pastor of First Church, New Haven) and great-granddaughter of Connecticut founder Thomas Hooker. Edwards’ responsibilities rapidly increased thereafter. He became a father in August 1728 with the birth of Sarah, the first of his eleven children.** **9** **Less than six months later, in February 1729, Stoddard died, leaving him in charge of the parish. The twenty-five-year-old Edwards was now, as George Marsden has aptly put it, “a man of authority”—an “aristocrat in a hierarchical society that took aristocracy for granted.”** **1**

This pronouncement was only faintly foreshadowed by the more polite Whiggery of Burgh’s suggested reading in “Oeconomics”: the **Spectator,**the **Tatler,**and the **Guardian**(**Youth’s Friendly Monitor,**first “Postscript” page).

**Edwards’ engagement with books during his Northampton and Stock-bridge pastorates is vividly revealed in the small, leather-bound “Account Book” he began keeping by 1733. Many of the entries, of interest to social and economic historians, are logs of money spent for muslin, wool, nails, sugar, tea, rum, chocolate, and other commodities. He also recorded salary received, debts incurred, marriages performed, and berry patches found. Interspersed with these entries is ample evidence of his role as both a consumer and a distributor of reading materials. Always an avid reader of newspapers, for example, he sent money to Boston for copies of the** **News-Letter** **and received other newspapers from the Dutch trader Abraham Fonda.** **4** **He also served as a middleman in the local book trade, several times brokering book transactions between an apparent colporteur, a Mr. Marshfield, and ministerial colleagues and parishioners.** **5** **Similarly, on more than a dozen occasions he procured English Bibles, presumably the King James Version, for resale to his parishioners, offering “great” Bibles for six pounds, five shillings, and “small” Bibles for one pound, ten shillings. After he became a published author, he sold, or sometimes gave away, copies of his own works: six of** **Religious Affections** **(1746), bound in calf; more than forty of** **An Humble Attempt** **(1747), both bound and unbound; an unspecified number of** **An Humble Inquiry** **(1749); and thirteen of** **Freedom of the Will** **(1754).** **6**

To a certain extent the kinds of books Edwards lent to the laity differentiate along predictable lines. A number of the titles lent to laypeople are pastoral treatises on everyday afflictions, such as Stephen Hales’ **Friendly Admonition to the Drinkers of Brandy**(1733), which he lent to “Dr Porters wife.” More ominously, Edwards lent the first volume of Thomas Mall’s **History of the Martyrs Epitomised**(Boston ed., 1747) “to steel a soldier” in August 1755, a few weeks after the French routed the British at Fort Duquesne. We also find evidence here that the old Puritan disease of “melancholy”—typically the result of excessive doubt about one’s eternal election—had not yet been eradicated by the antiseptic of liberalism. Thus Edwards lent to a layman Benjamin Colman’s **Case of Satan’s**

**But the most revealing entries in the “Account Book” are the many notations of books Edwards lent to family members, parishioners, and fellow clergy. These entries appear on nearly every page of the document, spanning the period from 1733, early in his Northampton pastorate, to 1757, as he was preparing to move from Stockbridge to Princeton. Though the manuscript is marred by several significant lacunae—evidently the handiwork of later souvenir seekers—the “Account Book” nevertheless provides a significant window into provincial book circulation patterns. Not only do we learn here what books Edwards actually owned, but we also see the book tastes of other local people, both clergy and laity. Of the lendees listed in the extant portions of the document, nearly 40 percent are Edwards’ fellow ministers. Of the remaining laypeople, nearly 30 percent are women. The 194 book-lending transactions recorded in the document, however, show that Edwards lent books far more often to clergy, several of whom borrowed quite frequently. Edwards’ younger protégé Samuel Hopkins tops the list, borrowing at least thirty titles, and probably more than fifty.** **7** **The secondmost-frequent borrower was Edwards’ other protégé, Joseph Bellamy, with twenty-one transactions, followed by Edwards’ father, Timothy, with ten. Three other ministers—Edward Billing, Jonathan Judd, and Cotton Mather Smith—borrowed roughly half a dozen books each, other clergy borrowing smaller numbers of titles.**

7. In over a dozen transactions, JE mentions simply “Mr. Hopkins,” not distinguishing between his protégé Samuel Hopkins (1721–1803), pastor at Great Barrington, Mass., and his brother-in-law Samuel Hopkins (1693–1755), pastor at West Springfield, Mass., though the younger man is probably meant in most of the cases. In at least 30 transactions, the younger Hopkins is clearly meant, either because the entry postdates the elder Hopkins’ death or because JE specifies Mr. Hopkins of “Houssetonock” (Housatonic) or “Sheffield” (both earlier names of Great Barrington).

<!-- p. 25 -->

**Not surprisingly, many of the books Edwards lent to clergy were related to theological controversies in New England. The reverberations from the Connecticut Apostasy were still being felt more than two decades later when Samuel Johnson, who after a sojourn in England had succeeded George Pigot as priest of the Anglican parish at Stratford, published** **A Letter from Aristocles to Authades** **(1745) condemning the Calvinist establishment’s doctrine of predestination as arbitrary and unjust.** **1** **Edwards shared his copy with Jonathan Judd, to whom he also lent Moses Dickinson’s** **Inquiry into the Consequences Both of Calvinistic and Arminian Principles** **(1750), a Calvinist attack on another Anglican apostate, John Beach. Soon thereafter Edwards lent to Samuel Hopkins** **A Second Address to the Members of the Episcopal Separation in New-England** **(1751) by the Congregationalist Noah Hobart, who continued the attack on Johnson, Beach, and other New England Anglicans. Meanwhile, as Calvinists were confuting the prelacy and Arminianism of the Anglicans, Arminian and other heresies were threatening from within the Congregational household. Thus, when a missionary to the Indians, Experience Mayhew, advocated a liberal policy of open communion and suggested that humans possess a measure of free will, Edwards shared the two offending books with fellow ministers.** **2** **One of the titles, Mayhew’s** **A Right to the Lord’s Supper Considered** **(1741), was newly relevant to Edwards’ Northampton situation when he lent the book to Joseph Bellamy in 1749. Edwards had just ended his grandfather Stoddard’s policy of open**

**Fiery Darts** **(1744), a work urging afflicted individuals to take comfort in their anxiety since it proved Satan hated them because they were elect.** **8** **Similarly, Edwards lent to a laywoman at Stockbridge** **Counsels and Comforts to Troubled Christians** **(1749), a work by his Scottish correspondent James Robe, who diagnosed the symptoms of melancholy and offered a step-by-step spiritual cure.** **9**

The disruptive effect of Croswell and other itinerants had prompted efforts by the authorities to regain control. Yet after Connecticut passed

**communion, declaring instead that the Lord’s Supper would henceforth be restricted to the truly godly. This move ultimately led to Edwards’ dismissal in 1750 and unleashed a new flurry of publications, including an attack the following year by the Arminian Robert Breck on one of Edwards’ defenders, William Hobby. Edwards lent Breck’s book, which he deemed “a great and very injurious representation” of his views, to Samuel Hopkins.** **3** **For Breck, however, it was payback time: Edwards had opposed his ordination during a protracted controversy in the 1730s.** **4**

**Breck’s book and the other controversial treatises circulated by Edwards prove that eighteenth-century New Englanders had not yet lost a sixteenth-century zeal for theological polemic. Indeed, the most colorful polemicist read by Edwards and his colleagues was Andrew Croswell, a radical New Light itinerant who believed he was leading “a second and glorious Reformation” by reviving the sixteenth-century message of justification by faith alone.** **5** **Croswell, who had earlier incensed the ministers of the Standing Order for defending the preaching of lay exhorters, caused a renewed stir when he settled as pastor of Boston’s Eleventh Church in mid-1746. In April of that year, Edwards lent to Jonathan Judd a copy of Croswell’s** **What Is Christ to Me, if He Is Not Mine?** **(1745), an attack on the old Puritan “preparationist” model of conversion, which emphasized the necessity of spiritual struggle and doubt over one’s election. To Croswell unconditional justification and, consequently, full assurance of salvation were the essence of Christianity, but to his opponents in the establishment such assurance smacked of the Antinomian heresy of a century earlier.** **6** **The establishment responded in force, for example in** **A Vindication of the Gospel-Doctrine of Justifying Faith** **(1746) by Edwards’ cousin and later nemesis Solomon Williams. Edwards lent Williams’ book to another protégé, John Searle, and also to his father, Timothy.**

**The old social distinctions between clergy and laity, and even to some extent between men and women, are further complicated when one analyzes the “Account Book” for the titles most frequently lent. Though eighteenth-century ministers often still inhabited an elite world of intra-clerical polemics, clergy and laity were increasingly driven by the same fashions in reading. Thus, of the eight books Edwards lent most frequently (four or more times), half are titles that might be termed polite,** **1** **and all but one of these he shared with both clergy and laity. Topping the list with eight transactions is** **The Ladies Library,** **the conduct book mentioned earlier, which Edwards lent to four women, two laymen, and two clergymen (Bellamy and Hopkins). The next most frequently lent is a theological title, the English Presbyterian Nathaniel Lardner’s** **Credibility of the Gospel History** **(1727–57), and Bellamy and Hopkins account for all six transactions. (Interestingly, Lardner’s seventeen-volume**

**a law in 1742 prohibiting anyone from preaching in a parish without the express invitation of “the settled minister or the major part of the church,” another member of the Williams clan, Solomon’s brother Elisha, weighed in on behalf of the itinerants and free speech. A minister, former rector of Yale College, onetime judge, and future militia colonel, Williams published anonymously** **The Essential Rights and Liberties of Protestants: A Seasonable Plea for the Liberty of Conscience and the Right of Private Judgment in Matters of Religion** **(1744), which drew on the ideas of religious toleration articulated by “the celebrated Lock[e].” In 1745 Edwards lent “Rector Wms Seasonable Plea” to Northampton parishioner Noah Clark—a significant citation because it helps confirm Williams’ authorship of the pamphlet, once disputed by historians.** **7** **That Edwards lent the book to a layman foreshadowed the laity’s increasing interest in natural rights, or the freedom from “any Controul from human Authority,” as Williams put it.** **8** **Such “natural rights” language signaled a growing shift away from the old covenant language of Puritanism, which privileged the clergy as arbiters of the covenantal terms.** **9** **This rhetorical and philosophical shift would not bode well for Edwards at Northampton.**

**Beyond these books lent at least four times, several other polite titles appear prominently in the “Account Book.” Edwards lent another conduct book, Defoe’s** **Family Instructor** **(1715–18), three times (once to Bellamy and twice to a laywoman). **Whiggish volumes account for nearly 20 percent of the transactions recorded in the “Account Book”—roughly double the percentage of individual polite titles listed in the “Catalogue.” Yet when the repeated citations in the “Catalogue” of polite periodicals such as the** **London Magazine** **and** **Republick of Letters** **are taken into account, the “Catalogue” too shows Edwards’ considerable familiarity with what people at the time called the “free and candid” or “catholick” spirit of polite European book culture.** **6**

**Edwards’ conversance with this culture would stand him in good stead when, after his dismissal from Northampton, he was invited in February 1751 to settle as minister in Stockbridge. Abigail Williams Sergeant, Edwards’ cousin and the young widow of the town’s previous pastor, was something of a theological liberal who enjoyed intellectual conversation and outfitted the Stockbridge mission house with the latest in elegant furnishings. Not predisposed in favor of Edwards, she was pleasantly surprised after conversing with him: “He is learned, polite, and free in conversation, and more catholic than I had supposed.”** **7** **Her brother Capt. Ephraim Williams, Jr., was far less sanguine, finding Edwards unsociable and “a very great bigot, for he would not admit any person into heaven, but those that agreed fully to his sentiments.”** **8** **Had Williams examined Edwards’ “Catalogue” and “Account Book,” however, he would have found that he and the minister shared many book interests. An inventory of Williams’ estate after he was killed in 1755 at the Battle of Lake George reveals that of the thirty-six books recorded, slightly more than half (nineteen) were also listed by Edwards in the “Catalogue” or “Account Book.”** **9** **Many of these titles are polite, Whiggish, Latitudinarian, or catholick in the broadest sense: Addison’s** **Freeholder,** **Addison and Steele’s** **Guardian** **and** **Spectator,** **Burnet’s** **History of the Reformation,**

9. See the full list of Williams’ books in Wyllis E. Wright, **Colonel Ephraim Williams: A Documentary Life**(Pittsfield, Mass., Berkshire County Historical Society, 1970), 163–66. Williams, who died unmarried, left much of his estate for the establishment of the school that became Williams College.

### The Hampshire Association Library

**Ephraim Chambers’** **Cyclopaedia,** **Harrington’s** **Oceana,** **Locke’s** **Works,** **Alexander Pope’s** **Works,** **1** **Paul de Rapin-Thoyras’** **History of England,** **and Trenchard and Gordon’s** **Independent Whig.** **(Williams took the last-named item with him into battle at Lake George, along with the New Testament and several other books.) To be sure, Williams did not share Edwards’ strong interest in scholastic treatises of Reformed divinity, yet clearly the two men were not as far apart in cultural and political knowhow as Williams (who once lamented of Edwards that “a head so full of divinity should be so empty of politics”) apparently assumed.** **2**

**The “Account Book” and “Catalogue” thus confirm that Edwards, no less than his colonial contemporaries, was a full-fledged participant in the European republic of letters. Indeed, the historian Henry F. May’s conclusion about colonial book reading—that it reveals “a remarkably catholic reception of European thought, with a certain time lag, and a clear preference for what was Protestant, Whiggish, moral, and moderate”** **3** **—might well describe book consumption at Edwards’ Northampton and Stockbridge parishes. The catholicity in colonial reading had its limits, of course, and Catholicism of the Roman variety was still beyond the pale. The “Account Book” lists several important anti-Catholic works: the two-volume** **History of Popery** **(1735–36); the multi-authored** **Sermons Against Popery, Preached at Salters-Hall** **(1735) and** **Morning-Exercise Against Popery** **(1675); and John Willison’s** **Popery, Another Gospel** **(1746). Yet anti-Catholic (and similarly, anti-Jacobite) language had become second nature to most English Protestants since the Glorious Revolution. It was in a peculiar way polite.**

Politeness and anti-Catholicism were among the themes that emerged in meetings of the Hampshire Association of Ministers, in which Edwards played a key role during his Northampton pastorate. Founded in 1714 by his grandfather Stoddard and his uncle William Williams, the two most influential ministers in Hampshire County, this ministerial association,

**Another way that groups such as the Hampshire Association cultivated the life of the mind was to establish libraries for their members’ common use. These social libraries, in which participants each paid a subscription fee, were then emerging in the colonies as the forerunners to public libraries. The advantages of social libraries were not only financial, since they mitigated the cost of book ownership for individuals, but also intellectual, since they created communities of people dedicated to literary self-improvement.** **6** **Benjamin Franklin and the fellow members of his Junto social club had founded what he later claimed was the first social library in America in Philadelphia in 1731.** **7** **It was soon followed**

**in acknowledging a “power in ecclesiastical councils,” marked a step toward presbyterian church government in western Massachusetts.** **4** **The group’s most important function was the examination and ordination of new ministers, although because this oversight lacked official state sanction it was occasionally resisted by local congregations, as in 1736 when the Arminian Robert Breck was ordained over the association’s objections by a council that included Boston-area ministers. In calmer times the Hampshire ministers convened on a regular basis to promote collegiality among themselves, and these meetings included indulging in debating exercises of the sort that most of the members had not participated in since college. At one meeting, for example, the Hampshire ministers took up the issue, “Are the Baptisms Administered by the Romish Clergie Valid?” The question was evidently so engaging that the ministers returned to it six months later and still found themselves “equally divided.”** **5**

**Though no full inventory of the Hampshire library is known to exist, some of the titles circulated can be gleaned from the association’s minutes. The library’s first recorded book, given by Edwards’ cousin and Longmeadow pastor Stephen Williams, revealed the ministers’ aspirations to inform themselves on subjects besides theology.** **Miscellanea Curiosa** **(1705–7) was a two-volume compilation of scientific treatises, many of them originally published in the** **Philosophical Transactions** **of the Royal Society of London, along with a third volume of travel accounts.** **1** **The scientific contributors included Isaac Newton and Edmond Halley, as well as the mathematicians John Craig, Abraham de Moivre, and John**

**by many others, including the Philogrammatican, organized in Lebanon, Connecticut, in 1738 by the town’s pastor and Edwards’ cousin Solomon Williams, along with future governor Jonathan Trumbull. Each member of the Lebanon library, including local ministers Thomas Clap, the future rector of Yale, and Eleazar Wheelock, the future founder of Dartmouth College, contributed fifty pounds for the purchase of books. The group also drew up a covenant of rules governing the library’s use and maintenance.** **8**

**By the time of the Lebanon library’s founding, the Hampshire ministers had been cooperating in a similar venture for six years. In 1732 they had agreed on a minimum subscription fee of ten pounds for their own library, which was to be used by the local clergy “of the Congregational or Presbyterian Perswasions, and other Benefactors.” Preference in borrowing was to be given to the highest benefactors, including Edwards and several others who had each given twenty pounds. No person was allowed to borrow more than the value of two folio volumes at one time. The library was to be divided between the northern and southern parts of the county, with the actual towns rotating, and all checked-out books were to be returned before each of the association’s twice-yearly meetings. Finally, to protect books while being transported by horse or carriage, each borrower was to be “furnished with a convenient wooden box, lined with paper or Cloth, wherein the Book may be carried & returned without Damage.”** **9**

**Meanwhile, polite works on religion were continuing to pique the ministers’ interest. In a “Catalogue” entry (no. 432) from around the same time as the 1738 meeting, Edwards mentions Joseph Addison’s** **Evidences of the Christian Religion** **(1730) as “a Book in the Springfield Library.” This posthumously published compilation included a preface “containing the Sentiments of Mr. [Robert] Boyle, Mr. Lock[e], and Sir Isaac Newton, concerning the Gospel-Revelation.” The book, which went through at least seven editions before Edwards’ death, exemplified the Latitudinarian, Lockean project of demonstrating the credibility of Christianity.** **4** **Axiomatic to this project was a belief in the necessity of divine revelation, given the limits of human reason. As the scientist Boyle put it elsewhere, “I cannot allow that the intellect of man is the genuine standard of truth,**

**Other correlations between the Hampshire library and Edwards’ notebooks are evident. In 1741 the library received at least one volume of Theophilus Gale’s four-volume** **Court of the Gentiles** **(1669–78).** **7** **Gale was a high Calvinist who had been ejected for nonconformity at the Restoration; he shared with the Latitudinarians and the Cambridge Platonists an interest in the necessity—and more important, the antiquity—of the Christian revelation. Through exhaustive philological erudition, Gale attempted to prove that Christianity’s fundamental truths had been imparted from the beginning to the ancient Jews and that this** **prisca theologia** **(ancient theology) was filtered down through Plato and other classical philosophers, whose writings contained vestiges of such biblical ideas as monotheism, the Trinity, and the immortality of the soul. Non-Jews like Plato thus received revelation in the “court of the Gentiles”—the outer courtyard of the ancient Jewish Temple in which Gentiles were permitted.** **8** **Edwards began copying passages from Gale in “Miscellanies,” no. 953, which dates from soon after the Hampshire library acquired the book.** **9** **He later copied long extracts from other works on the prisca theologia, especially the** **True Intellectual System of the Universe** **(1678) by the Cambridge Platonist Ralph Cudworth.** **1**

**Yet almost as soon as he was installed at Stockbridge in August 1751, Edwards clashed with the powerful Williams clan over the management of the mission. This local political intrigue has been recounted elsewhere, but suffice it to say that Edwards moved quickly to curry favor with powerful patrons.** **8** **One of these was the politician and military commander Sir William Pepperrell, the most influential New Light layman in the colonies, who had recently been feted by George II in London for leading the English to victory over the French at the Battle of Louisbourg in 1745. In November 1751, Edwards wrote a long letter to Pepperrell, who sat on the Massachusetts Council, detailing his philosophy for educating Indian children at the Stockbridge mission. In a surviving draft of the letter, he also penned a rough catalogue of books for pedagogical use. All eight of the books on the list also appear in Edwards’ larger “Catalogue.”** **9** **His recommendations included Dr. Samuel Johnson’s as yet**

**in Connecticut, Virginia, and even Scotland.** **4** **He also discouraged an effort by his son-in-law Col. Timothy Dwight to organize a rival church in Northampton.** **5**

**By the late 1740s, Edwards’ Scottish correspondents had replaced the Hampshire ministers as his most important contacts for obtaining books. In exchange he shared with them information on the progress of the gospel in America. In May 1749, he reported to John Erskine on the state of Indian missions and also commented on the recently founded College of New Jersey. Its president, the Rev. Aaron Burr, “is a man of religion and singular learning,” Edwards wrote, “and I hope the college will flourish under his care.” At the end of his letter, Edwards confided that a “very great difficulty has arisen between me and my people, relating to qualifications for communion at the Lord’s table.” The controversy over his discontinuation of Stoddard’s open communion policy had “filled all the country with noise” and was threatening to “issue in a separation between me and my people.”** **3**

The separation occurred the following June, when Edwards’ congregation dismissed him. The international prominence he had gained from such works as **A Faithful Narrative**was not enough to save him from his parishioners’ resentment and his own high-handedness. He continued to preach at Northampton over the next five months in the demoted status of supply pastor, apparently turning down job offers from congregations

Edward Braddock’s army at Fort Duquesne (Pittsburgh) heightened the apocalyptic mentality then rife among the English settlers.** **9** **Amid these tribulations, Edwards remained undeterred in his search for signs that papal Rome would soon**

**Pounds in lawful money of this Province, such as she shall chuse.” If none of their sons finished college, the entire library would be hers. Leaving books to sons rather than to daughters was typical of the time: John Sergeant had done the same, though his will allowed Abigail to select as many as she desired first.** **5**

**As for the size of Edwards’ library, an estate inventory prepared soon after his death listed, though not by titles, 301 volumes: 38 folios, 34 quartos, 99 octavos, and 130 duodecimos. Also listed were 536 pamphlets (which would have included sermons and other discourses printed in unbound form), as well as 25 copies of books written by Edwards himself.** **6** **All told, his collection was numerically comparable to those of other New England ministers, who typically acquired 200 or 300 volumes over the course of a career.** **7** **Truly large libraries were the luxury of a very few. Cotton Mather and the Virginia planter William Byrd II each owned more than 3,000 volumes at their deaths in 1728 and 1744, respectively. Boston’s Thomas Prince, who died the same year as Edwards, owned more than 1,500 volumes.** **8** **These men, however, had ready access to the seaport centers of colonial commerce and culture; Edwards accumulated books despite living much of his life on New England’s embattled frontier.**

**Meanwhile, Edwards’ strong interest in natural religion and the prisca theologia led him to copy long extracts in his notebooks from several authors. The most unlikely source was Andrew Michael Ramsay, known as Chevalier Ramsay, a Catholic and ardent anti-Calvinist who was created a baronet in the Jacobite court in exile on the Continent in 1735. Of the thousands of words Edwards penned in his “Miscellanies” in Stock-bridge, fully 10 percent of the material is copied from two of Ramsay’s works:** **Philosophical Principles of Natural and Revealed Religion** **(1748–49) and** **Travels of Cyrus** **(1727). Ramsay’s skill as an apologist for a universal Christianity, as well as his evidence for a pristine ancient wisdom that conformed to biblical religion, allowed Edwards to overlook his Catholic and Jacobite sympathies.** **8** **Similarly, Edwards disregarded the Anglicanism and Latitudinarianism of the Cambridge Platonist Ralph Cudworth, whose** **True Intellectual System of the Universe** **(1678) accounts for 9 percent of the material in the Stockbridge “Miscellanies.”** **9** **Edwards’ intense fascination with this text nearly eighty years after its original publication reveals the durability of Christian Platonism as a system purporting to identify a universal truth imparted to humankind from antiquity.** **1** **Cudworth (1617–88) was then enjoying something of a revival in England: a new two-volume edition of his** **True Intellectual System,** **including annotations on his sources and an account of his life, appeared in London in 1743.**
