### Edwards’ Book Interests: Major Categories

**Jersey governor Jonathan Belcher in 1750 had made the college’s library the sixth largest in the colonies, and by the time of Edwards’ appointment the collection probably included around 1,200 volumes.** **6** **Yet unlike his Yale days, Edwards’ tenure at Princeton afforded him all too little time for browsing among books. He died from a failed smallpox inoculation after only five weeks as president, with the college’s books lying unopened next door in Nassau Hall.** **7**

**In the foregoing pages, I have traced the trajectory of Edwards’ career with books. I turn now to an assessment of his reading habits by subject area and genre. Precisely how to classify his reading interests will always be debatable. Colonial libraries had no standard system of book classification such as the Library of Congress subject headings and call numbers used by most U.S. libraries today.** **8** **Eighteenth-century book collections, whether private or institutional, instead were classified according to the predilections of the collector. William Byrd II, for example, shelved his vast library according to eight categories, including “History, Voyages, Travels,” “Entertainment, Poetry, Translations,” “Divinity,” “French Books, Chiefly Entertainment,” and “Classicks, & Other Latin & Greek Authors.” Like other urbane Anglican aristocrats, he shared none of the early Puritans’ wariness of belletristic literature, which accounts for his large number of “Entertainment” titles, particularly drama.** **9** **By contrast, a catalogue of the Yale College library printed in 1743 included just half a page of “Plays and Books of Diversion” but nearly twenty pages of divinity books, arranged under fourteen subheads, including “Natural Religion,” “The Truth of the Scriptures,” and**

An inventory published two years later (in 1760) listed 1,281 volumes. See **A Catalogue of Books in the Library of the College of New-Jersey, January 29, 1760**(Woodbridge, N.J., 1760); and Alexander Leitch, **A Princeton Companion**(Princeton, Princeton Univ. Press, 1978), 285–86. The library’s status as sixth largest in 1750 is mentioned in an online history: http:// library.princeton.edu/about/history.php.

A few of JE’s own books became part of the Princeton library, thanks mostly to a late-nineteenth-century bequest. See Howard C. Rice, Jr., “Jonathan Edwards at Princeton: With a Survey of Edwards Materials in the Princeton University Library,” **Princeton University Library Chronicle**15–16 (1953–55), 69–89; and below, Appendix C.

A sense of the haphazard colonial practice of book classification may be gained from Robert B. Winans, **A Descriptive Checklist of Book Catalogues Separately Printed in America, 1693– 1800**(Worcester, American Antiquarian Society, 1981).

**Edwards’ bibliographical world certainly resembled Yale’s library more than Byrd’s, though as will be noted below, Edwards was not unlike Byrd in wanting to keep current with the latest developments in European book culture. “Polite Literature: The Republic of Letters” is therefore one of the categories employed below, owing not only to the ubiquity of polite titles in the “Catalogue” and “Account Book” but also to the currency of politeness as a concept in Edwards’ own cultural mi-lieu—the post-1688 world of Britain and its colonies.** **2** **Similarly, the other categories used below are designed to situate Edwards’ reading interests in cultural, intellectual, and religious history. Thus, Reformed (or Calvinist) books of divinity are discussed separately from non-Calvinist works, with the latter group including notable Anglican, Catholic, and Lutheran sources. “The Reasonableness of Christianity,” borrowing a title from John Locke, is treated as a separate category encompassing the many works in Edwards’ reading related to controversies over atheism, natural religion, deism, and the Trinity. For reasons to be explained below, works on the Bible, history, and politics are grouped together in a single category.Three other categories round out the discussions below: “Science and Mathematics” (the former was still called “Natural Philosophy” in Edwards’ day), “Books by Female Authors” (with particular attention to the role of women in the transatlantic evangelical network), and “Other Subjects and Genres” (a necessary catch-all for isolated titles of significance). The numerical representation of the most important categories within the roughly 632 separate book titles in the “Catalogue” and the 117 titles in the “Account Book” will be noted below, though the reader should bear in mind that these percentages are only approximate.** **3** **For determining them, no book title has been counted under more than one genre, but the best classification for certain books is debatable. The percentages for the “Account Book” are also subject to revision, should the remaining lacunae in the manuscript ever be filled by new discoveries.**

#### Reformed (Calvinist) Divinity

**Titles by ejected ministers occur frequently in Edwards’ “Catalogue” and “Account Book.” The reputations of these authors had been kept alive partly by Edmund Calamy (1671–1732), an English Presbyterian and the son and grandson of ejected ministers, who compiled hundreds of biographical sketches of deprived clergy in a popular account issued in 1702 and expanded in 1713 and 1727.** **5** **Calamy himself donated a copy of his account to Yale as part of the Dummer collection, and Edwards twice lists the work early in the “Catalogue” (nos. 81 and 202). Calamy originally published his biographies as an addendum to his abridged version of the autobiography of Richard Baxter (1615–91), who left the Church of England in protest just before the Act of Uniformity took effect. The prolific and doctrinally irenic Baxter, famous for**

**Works of Reformed divinity—including sermons, treatises, systematic theologies, and commentaries on specific portions of Scripture written in a Calvinist vein—are the most common genre in Edwards’ reading. Yet only about 20 percent of the individual titles listed in the “Catalogue,” and around 40 percent of the titles in the “Account Book,” fall into this category. The term “Reformed” is used here to denote the various traditions stemming from Huldrych Zwingli, Calvin, and their successors.** **4** **In the British Isles, these groups included not only those who acquired the epithet “Puritan” within the Elizabethan Church of England but also the various other dissenting parties adhering to Calvinist theology, including the Independents (known in America as Congregationalists), the Presbyterians, and the Particular Baptists. After the Restoration and the Act of Uniformity (1662), clergy in all these groups were denominated “Nonconformist” and deprived of their livings for failure to conform to the Church of England. The Act of Toleration (1689), part of William III’s anti-Catholic effort to unite Protestants, restored some of the ejected clergy’s earlier rights, but generations of dissenters nurtured the memory of the ejections.**

On the advantages of “Reformed” over “Calvinist” as broad designation, see Philip Benedict, **Christ’s Churches Purely Reformed: A Social History of Calvinism**(New Haven, Yale Univ. Press, 2002), xxii–xxiv.

Wykes, “‘To Let the Memory of These Men Dye Is Injurious to Posterity’: Edmund Calamy’s **Account**of the Ejected Ministers,” in **Studies in Church History, 33, The Church Retrospective,**ed. R. N. Swanson (Woodbridge, Boydell Press, 1997), 379–92. Wykes notes that Calamy’s **Account**was “part of a much older tradition of Protestant hagiography popularized by John Foxe’s **Acts and Monuments**and Samuel Clarke’s **Lives**” (p. 385). See JE’s references to Clarke and Foxe in “Catalogue” nos. 349 and 495. For a general summary of the Restoration settlements affecting the ejected clergy, see Benedict, **Christ’s Churches Purely Reformed,**408–22.

**Jonathan Edwards also read numerous Reformed writers born after the Restoration who consequently do not appear on Calamy’s list. Among his favorites was his contemporary Philip Doddridge (1702–51), an Independent minister in the moderate mold of Baxter. Doddridge died an untimely death at age forty-nine, though not before leaving an impressive published corpus. As will be discussed below, Edwards used Doddridge’s** **Family Expositor** **extensively, but he also listed several volumes of Doddridge’s practical theology and sermons in the “Catalogue.”** **6** **Another moderate Independent clergyman frequently read by Edwards was the hymn writer Isaac Watts (1674–1748), who has been described as “a study in hesitant Calvinism.”** **7** **Watts’ views on free will drew extensive criticism from Edwards in** **Freedom of the Will,** **but Edwards nevertheless admired Watts’ hymns and devotional works.**

**Another strong predestinarian in Edwards’ reading was John Gill (1697–1771), a Particular Baptist minister in London who was often classified as a “hyper-Calvinist” for his rejection of any evangelism based on the idea that God “offers” persons salvation. Edwards probably first learned of him in 1741, when the Hampshire Association acquired the two-volume set of Lime Street lectures, which included several of Gill’s sermons.** **1** **Edwards encountered his name again in 1748 when the** **Boston Gazette** **reported that Gill, “an eminent dissenting minister of the Baptist denomination,” had just received the doctor of divinity degree from the universities of Edinburgh and Glasgow (“Catalogue,” no. 494). Nicknamed “Dr. Voluminous” for the extent of his published corpus, Gill had in actuality just received the D.D. from Aberdeen in recognition of his ongoing** **Exposition of the Old and New Testaments,** **a commentary on every**

**Perhaps the most unusual Calvinist in Edwards’ reading was John Glas (1695–1773), founder of the Glasite (or Sandemanian) church in Scotland. Ordained a Presbyterian minister in 1719, Glas was deposed from the Church of Scotland eleven years later after publishing his opposition to state churches. Glas proceeded to gather a separate congregation at Dundee in an effort to restore the simplicity of the New Testament church. The community’s practices included the kiss of peace, foot washing, and weekly celebration of the Lord’s Supper. The Glasite movement would eventually come to America in 1764 when Glas’ son-in-law Robert Sandeman (1718–71), established several small congregations in Connecticut. Edwards probably learned of the movement from one of his Scottish correspondents. The “Account Book” reveals that he owned Glas’** **Notes on Scripture-Texts** **(1747), whose seven discourses included an explication of Romans 9 (in Number II) defending the Calvinist doctrine of predestination.** **8** **He also cites Glas’** **Notes** **elsewhere, including in the Table to the “Miscellanies.”** **9**

Murray, “John Glas,” in **ODNB.**JE lent Glas’ **Notes**to Hopkins, who, along with Joseph Bellamy, led the New Divinity’s opposition in the 1760s to Sandemanians and other alleged “antinomians” who denied the necessity of repentance prior to God’s gift of justifying faith. Twice in 1753 Edwards lent Hopkins “one vol. of Perkins,” presumably from the three-volume collected edition. Eleven editions of Perkins’** **Works** **had appeared in England between 1600 and 1635, and probate inventories from early New England reveal that it was not uncommon for seventeenth-century laypeople to own at least one volume of the set.** **6** **Yet no collected edition seems to have appeared after the 1630s, which means that Edwards’ copy was an antique not only because of its theology. **Even more important as sources for Edwards were prominent Anglicans from the other side of the Atlantic—figures such as John Tillotson and Samuel Clarke. Edwards’ willingness to engage their thought set him apart from the revivalist George Whitefield, who after a 1740 visit to Harvard famously sniffed that “Tillotson and Clark[e] are read instead of Shepard, Stoddard, and such like evangelical writers.”** **3** **Whitefield was**

Roughly 10 percent of the titles listed in the “Catalogue,” and 5 percent of the titles in the “Account Book,” are sermons and other theological works by non-Calvinist authors. The majority of these books are by Anglicans, though Catholics and Lutherans are also represented. The preponderance of Anglican sources is certainly due in part to Puritanism’s roots in the Church of England: the Puritan “godly” ministers of the sixteenth century were, after all, Anglican clergy. As we have seen, moreover, Edwards had early and formative exposure to Anglican thought, thanks to the Dummer collection at Yale and the Connecticut Apostasy of Cutler, Johnson, and colleagues in 1722. Their defection ignited intermittent pamphlet wars between New England Anglicans and Calvinists, as in 1732 when Jonathan Dickinson published **The Scripture-Bishop,**an anonymous defense of presbyterian ordination, which quickly prompted rebuttals from the Anglicans James Wetmore (one of the Connecticut apostates) and Arthur Browne (a Society for the Propagation of the Gospel missionary). Edwards noted this “Late Controversy” in the “Catalogue” (no. 367), in which he also listed works by other colonial Anglicans, including James Blair, founder of the College of William and Mary (no. 97), and James Honeyman, an SPG missionary in Rhode Island (no. 333).

**John Tillotson (1630–94) was reared in a Puritan household and always retained a desire to bridge the chasm between dissenters and conformists. During his education at Cambridge, however, he was converted to conformity and was ordained an Anglican priest around the time of the Restoration. He quickly gained popularity as a preacher and published a great number of sermons both individually and in six collections. After the Glorious Revolution, which he welcomed as a deliverance from popery, William III appointed him dean of St. Paul’s Cathedral. Once Archbishop of Canterbury William Sancroft was deposed for refusing to recognize William and Mary as monarchs, William appointed Tillotson archbishop and thus “primate of all England.”** **6** **Despite Edwards’ own ingrained New England aversion to episcopacy, he cited the archbishop’s sermons in various places—not only in** **Justification by Faith Alone** **but also in the “Miscellanies,” the “Notes on Scripture,” and the “Blank Bible.” Early in the “Catalogue” he listed Tillotson’s** **Works** **(no. 206) and later referred to another book as having been “written in dr. Tillotson’s Time” (no. 568). Tillotson was also quoted in various places in the** **Guardian,** **which, as we have seen, Edwards owned and circulated. Finally, Edwards read Tillotson—though possibly unwittingly—through several lengthy, anonymous extracts from his sermons in** **The Ladies Library.** **7**

He judged the archbishop to be “one of the greatest divines on the other side of the question”—the harbinger of a cultural shift away from Calvinism’s dim view of human nature and rationality.** **1** **Indeed, as Norman Fiering has persuasively argued, the Latitudinarian sermon, as exemplified by Tillotson, “was the primary medium by which New England was eased into the enlightenment.”** **2** **To be sure, Edwards and other intellectuals encountered Enlightenment philosophy more directly in the thought of such Anglicans as Clarke and Locke; their place in his reading will be discussed in later sections. Yet all three—Clarke, Locke, and Tillotson—partook of the same Latitudinarianism that bequeathed to the eighteenth century a new optimism about the power of human reason.**

Anglican Latitudinarianism also provided a theological rationale for moderate conformity, and Edwards was familiar with these defenses of the Church of England and its government, especially in light of the Yale apostasy of Cutler, Johnson, and colleagues. Early in the “Catalogue” (no. 10), he mentions the “B[isho]p of Bangor”—namely, Benjamin Hoadly (1676–1761), who as a young man had published **The Reasonableness of Conformity to the Church of England**(1703), one of the texts that later influenced the apostates. Hoadly’s book was a response to Edmund Calamy, who had defended dissenting separation in his 1702 abridgment of Richard Baxter’s autobiography. A second exchange between the two authors ensued, in which Hoadly incensed Nonconformists by arguing that they should submit to episcopal reordination for the sake of church unity. Yet after his consecration in 1716 as bishop of Bangor, Hoadly angered the high-church party with a pair of publications denying the church’s authority over individual conscience. These publications included a sermon, **The Nature of the Kingdom, or Church, of Christ**(1717), delivered before King George I and printed at his command—a royal

**imprimatur that aroused suspicions among high churchmen that the Whiggish Hoadly was moving dangerously close to Erastianism (the idea that the state exercises supremacy over the church in ecclesiastical matters). The result was the protracted “Bangorian Controversy,” in which the lower house of the Convocation of Canterbury moved to condemn Hoadly, to which the king responded by terminating the Convocation’s session. Edwards was aware of this controversy: the “Miscellanies” include an apparent reference to Hoadly’s** **Nature of the Kingdom,** **and the “Catalogue” includes an entry on his** **Answer** **to the lower house of Convocation (no. 186).** **3**

Hoadly’s controversial defense of individual conscience—and his claim that true religion lay in a “sincerity” that only Christ could judge— upset even some of his Whig allies in the episcopate. He thus acquired a reputation for being at the far left wing of the Anglican hierarchy. Edwards’ reading interests, meanwhile, covered the full continuum of opinion among the Church of England’s bishops. A number of prelates mentioned in the “Catalogue” were elevated to the episcopate by Queen Anne, whose accession in 1702 upon the death of William III pushed the Church of England in a high-church direction. William Beveridge (listed in no. 55), bishop of St. Asaph, Wales, was a high churchman who opposed the 1707 Act of Union between England and Scotland (which Anne supported) because of the presbyterianism of the Scottish church. George Bull (nos. 87 and 135), bishop of St. David’s, Wales, who attempted in one treatise to reconcile Paul’s emphasis on faith with James’ emphasis on works, earned an unusual tribute from the Catholic clergy of France for his works defending Nicene orthodoxy. Ofspring Blackall (no. 531), bishop of Exeter, opposed Benjamin Hoadly and argued that the clergy’s spiritual authority was based on divine right. Sir William Dawes (no. 51), successively bishop of Chester and archbishop of York, was another Tory opponent of Hoadly and reputedly the best preacher of his day. Charles Hickman (no. 389), bishop of Derry, was a leading high churchman in the Anglican Church of Ireland. Finally, John Sharp (no. 257), though appointed archbishop of York by William III, was a high churchman who became a close spiritual adviser of Queen Anne.

**A final noteworthy Anglican prelate in Edwards’ reading is Thomas Sherlock (1677–1761), bishop successively of Bangor, Salisbury, and London. Sherlock is perhaps best known for his anti-deist works, which Edwards used, but the “Account Book” reveals that Edwards also circulated a sermon Sherlock preached after two earthquakes struck the London area in 1750. As bishop of London, Sherlock had spiritual oversight of the American colonies—a daunting task that prompted him to campaign for the installation of a resident American bishop. His effort ultimately failed, but not before exciting suspicions in New England that Sherlock was in league with Timothy Cutler as part of an Anglican conspiracy.** **5**

**Quietism and Jansenism—that were in some respects amenable to Protestantism. Both movements had run afoul of France’s absolutist monarch Louis XIV, which lent them a certain legitimacy among Protestants, who reviled the Sun King as the epitome of Catholic tyranny.** **2** **Quietism, most often associated with the Spanish priest Miguel de Molinos (1628–96), emphasized passive contemplation and annihilation of the self in order to achieve a disinterested love of God. Like Protestantism, Quietism rejected a works-based theology of salvation and the authority of the institutional church over the individual soul. In France two popular spiritual writers were influenced by Quietism: Jeanne Marie Bouvier de la Motte (1648–1717), better known as Madame Guyon; and François de Salignac de la Mothe Fénelon (1651–1715), the archbishop of Cambrai. Guyon’s writings were condemned by the church in 1695. The “Account Book” instead reflects the long heritage, common to Puritans and most Anglicans at the time, of antipathy toward Romanism, with several major anti-Catholic works appearing: Henry Care’s **History of Popery**(1735–36); a collection of Salters Hall lectures, **Sermons Against Popery**(1735); Nathaniel Vincent’s **Morning-Exercise Against Popery**(1675); and John Willison’s **Popery, Another Gospel**(1746). These texts helped stoke the periodic fears in England and the colonies of a Jacobite conspiracy to reinstall a Catholic king.

#### The Reasonableness of Christianity

Not long after Cudworth’s own death in 1688, the cause of reasonable Christianity received a new boost, thanks to a bequest from Robert Boyle

**At least 10 percent of the titles in both the “Catalogue” and the “Account Book” stem from the many post-Restoration debates in England over atheism, natural religion, deism, and the Trinity. Many of these books were defenses of the reasonableness of Christianity, written for a broad audience and motivated by a perceived groundswell of unbelief. This widespread fear of infidelity and even atheism arose from a complex confluence of factors after 1660. Even as the established church benefited from a backlash against Puritan radicalism, a new anti-religious radicalism, epitomized by the philosophy of Thomas Hobbes, now seemed to threaten Christianity’s very foundations. Hobbes became the symbol of an “atheistic” determinism in which individuals were governed by purely physical desires and appetites and thus, according to his** **Leviathan** **(1651), had to be held in check by an absolute human sovereign. Less immediately threatening to religion but no less momentous in the long run was the emergence after the Restoration of Newtonian physics, with its laws of motion and gravitation, which made God’s previously unpredictable providence more predictable. The Restoration also reinvigorated a culture of coffee-house and tavern freethinking, which helped spawn a literary renaissance of satire and wit. Amid all of these developments, a number of important thinkers rushed to defend Christianity against scoffers both real and imagined and to prove that biblical theism was not incompatible with science or reason.** **8**

**Leading the charge against the “atheists” of the day were the Cambridge Platonists, particularly Ralph Cudworth, whose** **True Intellectual System of the Universe** **(1678) traced the Christian idea of God to pre-Christian antiquity. The engraved frontispiece of this folio depicted the victory of theists over “atheists” such as Epicurus, whose atomism and its modern successor in mechanical philosophy Cudworth sought to replace with a Christianized atomism.** **9** **Edwards, as we have seen, was an avid consumer of the** **True Intellectual System;** **we can only speculate on how he might have used the long extracts he copied in 1757, just months before his death.**

Regarded as the father of modern chemistry, Boyle was a deeply religious scientist who sought throughout his career to demonstrate God’s design of the universe with evidence from the book of nature.** **1** **In his will Boyle provided for the establishment of an annual series of eight lectures “for proving the Christian religion against notorious infidels.” The inaugural Boyle lecturer in 1692 was the young Richard Bentley (1662–1742), a priest who would later gain his greatest fame as a classicist. In lecture seven of his series, Bentley drew on personal correspondence with Isaac Newton to defend a Christianized atomism—a world held together by divinely superintended gravity—against Epicurean philosophy.** **2** **The “Account Book” reveals that Edwards owned the published edition of Bentley’s lectures,** **The Folly and Unreasonableness of Atheism** **(1693), lending it once to his father and once to another minister. He probably also had Bentley’s work at hand when, during his graduate studies in New Haven, he noted in his “Natural Philosophy” papers that “it is universally allowed that gravity depends immediately on the divine influence.”** **3**

Boyle was confident that the new mechanical philosophy would reinforce the traditional doctrine of providence. See Michael P. Winship, **Seers of God: Puritan Providentialism in the Restoration and Early Enlightenment**(Baltimore, Johns Hopkins Univ. Press, 1996), 42–43, 64.

Yet these works were not enough to prevent natural religion’s most radical students, the deists, from rejecting the biblical God in favor of Nature’s God. The orthodox cultivation of natural religion thus had the unintended consequence of incubating a persistent new strain of unorthodoxy.

**Edwards’ fascination with the Boyle Lectures reflected his wider interest in works on natural religion. By the early eighteenth century, “natural religion” meant more than simply proving God’s existence through logical argumentation—the enterprise familiar to medieval systematicians as natural theology.** **7** **Natural religion in Edwards’ day was a catchphrase for the myriad attempts to marshal the resources of the new learning—Newtonian physics, cosmology, comparative religion—to demonstrate God’s existence through sheer weight of scholarly evidence. Most of the proponents of natural religion known to Edwards believed that it could be reconciled perfectly with revealed religion (the Bible). The titles of the works speak for themselves. Among the more important examples listed in the “Catalogue” are Joseph Butler’s** **Analogy of Religion, Natural and Revealed** **(no. 492); Chevalier Ramsay’s** **Philosophical Principles of Natural and Revealed Religion** **(no. 605); John Ray’s** **Three Physico-Theological Discourses** **(no. 249); Arthur Ashley Sykes’** **Principles and Connexion of Natural and Revealed Religion** **(no. 645); William Warburton’s** **Principles of Natural and Revealed Religion** **(no. 659; also listed in the “Account Book”); and William Whiston’s** **Astronomical Principles of Religion, Natural and Reveal’d** **(no. 216).**

The quest for natural religion was not without peril for orthodoxy. The potential always existed that natural religion’s zealous proponents would finally judge revealed religion less reliable or even superfluous. Consequently, apologies for the reliability and necessity of the Scriptures abounded, and a number of them appear in the “Catalogue,” including Joseph Addison’s **Evidences of the Christian Religion**(no. 432); Robert Jenkin’s **Reasonableness and Certainty of the Christian Religion**(no. 213); Nathaniel Lardner’s **Credibility of the Gospel History**(no. 447); John Locke’s **Reasonableness of Christianity as Delivered in the Scriptures**(no. 344); and Sir Charles Wolseley’s **Reasonableness of Scripture-Belief**(no. 692).

**The harbinger of deism was the Irish freethinker John Toland (1670–1722), who in** **Christianity Not Mysterious** **(1696) argued that true Christianity could not require the belief in mysteries, or things contrary to human reason.** **9** **Toland’s friend Anthony Collins (1676– 1729) extended this logic—and contradicted his other friend John Locke—by arguing in** **A Discourse of the Grounds and Reasons of the Christian Religion** **(1724) that it was contrary to reason that Old Testament prophecies were literally fulfilled in Jesus. The argument from fulfilled prophecy was a time-honored apologetic strategy in Christianity, but Collins maintained that Hebrew prophecies at best applied to Jesus in “a secondary, or typical, or mystical, or allegorical sense”—modes of interpretation he found dangerously arbitrary.** **1** **Other deists included the onetime Roman Catholic Matthew Tindal (1657–1733), who argued in** **Christianity as Old as the Creation** **(1731) that “Men of Good Sense” needed no supernatural revelation and that natural religion transcended the polemical distortions of revealed religions.** **2** **Meanwhile, the defrocked Independent minister and sometime physician Thomas Morgan (d. 1743) continued the deist attack on the Bible in** **The Moral Philosopher** **(1737). Anticipating the later polemics of Thomas Paine’s** **Age of Reason** **(1795), Morgan depicted the Old Testament God as a local tyrant and Jewish patriarchs such as David as wholly given over to “Dissimulation, Falsehood, Lust and Cruelty.”** **3**

In rushing anew to the defense of biblical religion, these orthodox attacks on deism reflected a strong commitment to the Protestant principle of “Scripture alone.” Yet paradoxically, this back-to-the-Bible mentality led some of the orthodox into a different kind of unorthodoxy: a belief that the Trinity—that most metaphysical of the church’s doc-trines—lacked biblical justification. Doubts about the Trinity had ancient roots in Christianity. Key clauses of the Nicene Creed were written to confute Arius, a fourth-century North African priest who taught that Jesus could not have been of one substance with the unknowable and immutable God. Jesus, as the subordinate Son made by God, was both knowable and mutable, even while remaining glorious and superior to humankind. More than a millennium after Arius, the Italian theologian Faustus Socinus (1539–1604) also rejected the triune God of Nicaea,

**the entries deal directly or indirectly with deism.** **5** **He also knew about or read dozens of orthodox responses to the leading deists, many of which appear in the “Catalogue.” Anthony Collins elicited the most responses, among which Edwards lists Richard Bentley’s** **Remarks upon a Late Discourse of Free-Thinking** **(no. 569), Edward Chandler’s** **Defence of Christianity from the Prophecies of the Old Testament** **(no. 305), Samuel Chandler’s** **Vindication of the Christian Religion** **(no. 553), John Gill’s** **Prophecies of the Old Testament Respecting the Messiah** **(no. 556), William Harris’** **Principal Representation of the Messiah Throughout the Old Testament** **(no. 325), Thomas Jeffery’s** **True Grounds and Reasons of the Christian Religion** **(no. 557), Thomas Sherlock’s** **Use and Intent of Prophecy** **(no. 469), and Arthur Ashley Sykes’** **Essay upon the Truth of the Christian Religion** **(no. 573).** **6** **Responses to Matthew Tindal include John Conybeare’s** **Defence of Reveal’d Religion** **(no. 586), John Leland’s** **Answer to a Late Book Intituled, Christianity as Old as the Creation** **(no. 699), and George Trumbull’s** **Philosophical Enquiry Concerning the Connexion Betwixt the Doctrines and Miracles of Jesus Christ** **(no. 641). Finally, rebuttals of Thomas Morgan include John Chapman’s** **True Christian’s Defense Against a Late Book Entitul’d The Moral Philosopher** **(no. 588), John Leland’s** **Divine Authority of the Old and New Testament** **(no. 677), and Moses Lowman’s** **Civil Government of the Hebrews** **(no. 500).**

**Sherlock’s travails confirmed the dictum of Adam of St. Victor (“Of the Trinity to reason/leads to license or to treason”)** **2** **and foreshadowed the more famous Arian Controversy involving the theologian Samuel Clarke (1675–1729). Though he denied embracing Arianism or Socinianism, Clarke examined more than twelve hundred relevant New Testament passages and concluded in his** **Scripture-Doctrine of the Trinity** **(1712)**

**this time on scriptural grounds.** **7** **Socinus, who had joined the Anabaptist movement in Poland and had adopted its biblical primitivism, insisted that the Trinity lacked convincing scriptural warrant—a contention supported by textual studies, which had proven that one of the chief Trinitarian proof-texts, I John 5:7 (the so-called** **Comma Johanneum** **),** **8** **was not present in any early New Testament manuscripts.**

**Anti-Trinitarianism was pioneered in England by the Unitarian schoolmaster John Biddle (1615–62), who probably produced the English translation of the Socinians’ Racovian Catechism that appeared in London in 1652.** **9** **Banished by Oliver Cromwell in 1655 and arrested upon his return, Biddle ultimately died in prison. Over the next several decades, sporadic Trinitarian debate continued, prompted by occasional treatises, including a 1685 anti-Socinian work,** **Defensio Fidei Nicaenae** **(“Catalogue,” no. 675), by George Bull, later bishop of St. David’s. A new controversy erupted in the 1690s after William Sherlock, soon to be John Tillotson’s successor as dean of St. Paul’s, published his** **Vindication of the Doctrine of the Holy and Ever Blessed Trinity** **(1690). Intended as an antidote to Socinianism, Sherlock’s work instead raised questions about his own views, which opponents likened to tritheism, or the belief in three separate gods. The affair prompted William III, at the urging of Archbishop of Canterbury Thomas Tenison, to forbid the use of “new” terms related to the Trinity.** **1**

#### Polite Literature: the Republic of Letters

**orthodox Congregationalism in many New England parishes by the early nineteenth century. Yet ironically, as we have seen, theological liberalism was the unintended byproduct of the orthodox clergy’s own zeal for “reasonable” Christianity. The deist Anthony Collins’ reputed quip in reference to Samuel Clarke’s Boyle Lectures aptly expresses the predicament of the time: nobody doubted the existence of God until Dr. Clarke sought to prove it.** **8**

**Much has been written by historians and social scientists on the role of the polite republic of letters in the creation of the bourgeois public sphere. Its chief institution was the coffee house—by the first decade of the eighteenth century, London alone had more than three thousand— and its archetypal literary organs were Addison and Steele’s** **Spectator** **and** **Guardian.** **1** **Though Edwards’ Northampton was removed from the Old World metropolises, the kinds of books one might hear discussed in a European kaffeeklatsch were hardly unknown to readers in the colonies. Indeed, the attraction of Edwards and his circle to the republic of letters is evident from the fact that when repeat lending transactions are taken**

**In his preface to** **Discourses on Various Important Subjects** **(1738), Edwards explained that because of the urgency of preaching the gospel, he shunned “such ornaments as politeness, and modishness of style and method.”** **9** **Yet despising politeness in preaching was one thing; despising politeness in reading was quite another. Indeed, nearly 10 percent of the titles in “Catalogue” and “Account Book” are titles that may be classified as polite. As used here, the term “polite” encompasses the various emerging genres of the eighteenth-century culture of exchange known as the “republic of letters.” These new genres included literary periodicals, encyclopedic works, conduct books, epistolary novels, newspapers, and other compilations. Though some of these works might be classified as belles lettres (typically defined as “light” literature read chiefly for entertainment), many of them also served as vehicles for education and edification. Indeed, Edwards rarely, if ever, approached the republic of letters as an end in itself but rather saw it as a means of gaining knowledge that could be reapplied for his own evangelical purposes.**

Stromberg, **Religious Liberalism,**10.

**Edwards’ interest in such literature began early. During his Yale tutorship, in the same note in which he resolved to “play at small games first” before publishing in London, he also resolved to follow the rules for writing outlined in** **The Ladies Library.** **Among the rules was this Enlightenment dictum: “Judge no farther than you perceive, and take not any thing for Truth, which you do not evidently know to be so.”** **2** **The youthful Edwards’ fascination with the rhetoric and logic of** **The Ladies Library** **resembles the young Benjamin Franklin’s attraction to the language of the** **Spectator,** **which he adopted as a model for writing while apprenticing as a printer with his brother in Boston.** **3** **Both Edwards and Franklin testify to the popularity of polite literary compilations in the early eighteenth century.**

**But Edwards’ favorite work of this type was by the man known in England as the “Father of Cyclopaedias,” Ephraim Chambers (1680?– 1740). Originally apprenticed to a mapmaker, Chambers abandoned this career in favor of the lifelong compilation of miscellaneous knowledge.** **7** **Edwards sent for Chambers’ magnum opus in 1737, and his surviving letter to the Boston merchant Jacob Wendell reveals his impatience to receive his order. “I want very much to know whether you have seen cause to comply with my request,” Edwards entreated, “that I may order my business accordingly.” Two weeks later, he received word through a middleman that the books were on their way. “I am very glad of it,” he wrote to Wendell, “and very thankful to you.”** **8** **We can only imagine his exhilaration when the order finally arrived in Northampton. Published in London in 1728, the heavy pair of folio volumes boasted a paragraph-length title headed by the sweeping claim:** **Cyclopaedia; or, An Universal Dictionary of Arts and Sciences; Containing the Definitions of the Terms, and Accounts of the Things Signify’d Thereby, in the Several Arts, Both Liberal and Mechanical, and the Several Sciences, Human and Divine.**

**distinctions and willingly assisted one another in the pursuit of knowledge, beauty, and truth. Yet this spirit also gave rise to much wider ranging—and more religiously questionable—works foreshadowing modern-day encyclopedias. The pioneering achievement of this genre was the** **Grand dictionnaire** **(1671) of Louis Moréri (1643–80), a French Jesuit priest, whose defenses of the Catholic Church prompted a rival encyclopedia, the** **Dictionnaire historique et critique** **(1697) by the Huguenot Pierre Bayle.** **6** **Edwards first lists Bayle in “Catalogue,” no. 236, and he lists the English adaptation of Moréri by Jeremy Collier in no. 294.**

Edwards soon began combing the **Cyclopaedia**for references to other books he might acquire. René Descartes’ **Discours de la méthode**(1637), he noted to himself, is commended by Chambers as “an incomparable Treatise.” Francis Hutcheson’s **An Inquiry into the Original of Our Ideas of Beauty and Virtue**(1725) “seems a very ingenious thing by the specimens of this Book in Chambers.” Christian Wolff’s **Elementa Matheseos Universae**(1713) “is a work never Enough to be Commended,” according to

**Even after acquiring Chambers, Edwards continued to follow similar reference texts appearing on the market. Soon after Denis Diderot and Jean le Rond d’Alembert published the first installment of their famous** **Encyclopédie** **(1751–72), Edwards recorded the title in the “Catalogue” (no. 618). Originally begun as a French translation of Chambers, the** **Encyclopédie** **became a groundbreaking work in its own right, with new articles by such Enlightenment luminaries as Baron d’Holbach, Jean-Jacques Rousseau, and Voltaire. Edwards learned of the** **Encyclopédie** **from an article in the London** **Monthly Review,** **and though it is likely he never obtained any of the volumes—he did not read French in any case—his interest in the work prefigures the later industry of Enlightenment publishing in the era of the French Revolution.** **4**

**Chambers.** **9** **Indeed, throughout his later career, Edwards returned to Chambers periodically for ideas both metaphysical and practical. In his “Miscellanies,” he cited Chambers for evidence of beliefs about hell among the philosophers of classical antiquity.** **1** **In a 1746 letter to an unknown correspondent, he invoked Chambers on the multiple philosophical senses of the word** **nature.** **2** **And writing from Stockbridge to Scottish correspondent William McCulloch in 1752, he lamented that the local Indians were neglecting public worship to scour the woods for ginseng root—a plant, he noted, described in Chambers—to sell to traders in Albany.** **3**

No less than encyclopedias, periodicals were crucial to the spread of Enlightenment ideas in the transatlantic republic of letters. Some encyclopedists, such as Pierre Bayle and Ephraim Chambers, were also periodical editors. Bayle’s journal, **Nouvelles de la République des Lettres**(1684), helped give the republic of letters its name, while Chambers’ **Literary Magazine**(1735) similarly offered news of the latest books. Edwards, as we have seen, eagerly combed periodicals such as the **Present State of the Republick of Letters,**the **London Magazine,**and the **Monthly Review**for new book references. He also, as noted earlier, enjoyed the polite style of moderate Whig periodicals such as Addison and Steele’s **Guardian,**which prompted him to add to his “Catalogue” wish list a number of

**Edwards was an equally eager consumer of colonial newspapers such as the pioneering** **Boston Weekly News-Letter,** **the** **Boston Gazette,** **the** **Boston Evening-Post,** **and the** **New-York Gazette.** **At first filled mostly with reports reprinted from London, American newspapers helped anglicize readers in the polite culture of the mother country. By the 1730s, colonial newspapers were coming into their own as forums for discussion among the colonists. The tours of George Whitefield beginning in 1739 greatly increased the frequency—and rancor—of printed debates as colonists quarreled over the propriety of the revivals.** **5** **Paradoxically, though American journalism emerged amid a transatlantic vogue of sociability and politeness, it also created a new public space for contention and even hatred. An example of the darker potential of the press occurs in “Catalogue,” no. 660, where Edwards cites a reference to the works of the Anglican Thomas Jackson from an anonymous letter printed in the** **Boston Evening-Post.** **Though Edwards does not mention it, the letter invokes anti-Jewish comments by Jackson and concludes: “Wolves and Bears will become mild as Domestick Creatures, by being housed and fed: The Jews alone, of all Animals, when harboured and well treated, grow more venomous and cruel.”** **6** **The printing of such scurrilous material foreshadowed the unfettered world of nineteenth- and early-twentieth-century American journalism, when organs such as Henry Ford’s** **Dearborn Independent** **popularized a virulent anti-Semitism.**

similar organs from the same era: the **Spectator**(no. 241), the **Englishman**(no. 242), the **Freeholder**(no. 243), the **Lover**(no. 255), and the **Reader**(no. 255).

**Finally, and quite significant, we also find in Edwards’ reading the first glimmers of another modern phenomenon: the novel. Readers today are accustomed to novels of many moods and styles, but in Edwards’ day this nascent genre was chiefly a conveyor of polite moral lessons. The book historian Kevin J. Hayes has aptly called the proto-novels of Edwards’ day “didactic fictional discourses,” and the prototype was Samuel Richardson’s** **Pamela,** **published in four volumes in 1740–41.** **7** **Like the heroine of his novel, Richardson (1689–1761) was not a product of polite society. Born to a working-class family, he apprenticed to a printer and gained early writing experience as the author of a book of sample letters designed to teach the semi-literate how to conduct business and**

**Boston Evening-Post,**April 1, 1754, p. 1.

**Richardson knew that the English public was largely unaccustomed to fiction, and many people regarded it as immoral. The novel’s title page thus billed** **Pamela** **as a book designed to “cultivate the Principles of Virtue and Religion in the Minds of the Youth of Both Sexes.” Richardson’s strategy proved wildly successful. Almost immediately,** **Pamela** **went through multiple printings and also took the American colonies by storm, prompting one Philadelphian to observe in the winter of 1741– 42 that “** **Pamela** **was in everybody’s mouth and happy the person who could procure a reading.”** **9** **Edwards was among these eager colonial readers, though** **Pamela** **does not surface in the “Catalogue” until 1751 (no. 593). Soon thereafter, he procured his own copy and lent it to friends five times between 1754 and 1756. His twenty-three-year-old daughter Esther Edwards Burr also read** **Pamela** **during this period and recorded her reactions in a series of letters to her friend Sarah Prince, daughter of the Boston minister Thomas Prince. Though Esther found some of the novel’s discourses admirable, she also found its heroine more than a little unbelievable. “Pray my dear how could Pamela forgive Mr. B. all his Devilish conduct so as to consent to marry him?” she wrote. “Sertainly this does not well agree with so much virtue and piety.”** **1** **Esther’s reflective letters to Sarah mirrored the epistolary form of** **Pamela** **itself and epitomized the polite intellectual exchange idealized by the republic of letters.** **2**

**personal communications.** **8** **He continued this epistolary form in** **Pamela,** **which narrates the fictional story of Pamela Andrews, a servant girl, who is doggedly pursued by Mr. B., the son of her late mistress, who temporarily confines her in his country estate under the watchful eye of the cruel Mrs. Jewkes. Mr. B. eventually repents of his behavior, and he and Pamela are reconciled and married. Though in the novel’s final two volumes Mr. B. has an affair with another woman, Pamela’s enduring patience and virtue lead him again to repent and pledge his unwavering fidelity—hence the novel’s subtitle,** **Virtue Rewarded.**

**Because early editions of** **Pamela** **appeared anonymously, Esther mistakenly referred to its author as “Mr. Fielding”—an ironic slip since Henry Fielding had actually written a humorous parody of Richardson’s novel entitled** **An Apology for the Life of Mrs. Shamela Andrews** **(1741). Edwards also knew of Fielding and listed his last novel,** **Amelia** **(1751), in the “Catalogue” (no. 610), noting that it was “much commended” in the** **Monthly Review** **“as recommending vertue and Conjugal Love.” There is no evidence that Edwards actually read any works by Fielding (1707– 54), whose comic characters—especially the lovable but lustful Tom Jones—were less appealing to sober New Englanders than Richardson’s wholly virtuous protagonists. (Not surprisingly, William Byrd II of Virginia owned** **Tom Jones.** **)** **3** **Richardson’s novels, however, were not without titillating aspects. Indeed, his fiction is unique among the books Edwards read in its suggestive portrayal of lascivious behavior. Fielding had in fact scornfully attributed the popularity of Richardson’s novels to the titillation they provided, and some more prudish readers had deemed** **Pamela** **’s “warm scenes” unfit for proper ladies.** **4** **These included scenes of Mr. B. and the manly Mrs. Jewkes forcing themselves upon Pamela, interspersed with occasional sexual innuendo.** **5** **This bawdy content was enough for Sir Leslie Stephen to suggest erroneously in an 1873 article that the offending volume in the Northampton “Bad Book” episode (which helped doom Edwards) was** **Pamela.** **6** **Yet to Edwards’ evident approval, virtue triumphs in the novel’s conclusion, when Pamela proves, in the spirit of Christian egalitarianism, that “my Soul is of equal Importance with the Soul of a Princess.”** **7**

**Robinson Crusoe** **provides an appropriate segue to the present section, in which history is the central theme. When Defoe asserted in the preface to his famous novel that it was “a just History of Fact; neither is there any Appearance of Fiction in it,” he was writing at a pregnant moment in English culture.** **1** **The emergence of the genre of the novel, with its history-like appearance, was prompting new reflections on the boundaries between fact and fiction. Intellectuals before the eighteenth century had pondered the factual nature of historical narrative, but by Edwards’ day the problem of the** **biblical** **narratives’ historicity was emerging in sharp relief.** **2** **The fact-fiction dichotomy would become the primary lens for judging Scripture, whose traditional claim to ultimate truth would not fare well in some sectors of the new critical economy. Though Edwards lived in this transitional time and sensed the interpretive shift taking place, the precritical historical assumptions he inherited from Puritanism**

As Stephen J. Stein has shown, Edwards relied principally on three synoptic commentators, all of them Nonconformist divines: Matthew Poole, Matthew Henry, and Philip Doddridge.** **5** **Poole (1624–79) entered the ministry during the Commonwealth period but resigned his preferment after the Restoration and the Act of Uniformity. Originally he had planned to undertake a large collection of accounts of remarkable divine providences, an idea later taken up in America by Increase Mather.** **6** **Instead, Poole spent the last decade of his life writing learned synopses from the Catholic, Protestant, and Jewish commentarial tradition on every book of the Bible. This massive Latin opus became the** **Synopsis Criticorum** **(5 vols., 1669–76), which Edwards lists in the “Catalogue” only once (no. 151) but cites in the “Blank Bible” an astounding 792 times, more than any other source. Henry (1662–1714) was an English Presbyterian and popular evangelical preacher whose** **Exposition of the Old and New Testament** **(6 vols., 1707–21) was intended to cover the whole Bible but was cut short by his death. **still held sway over his everyday imagination.** **3** **In his view, extra-biblical works of history were not qualitatively different from the Bible itself in that both conveyed factual events guided by divine providence. Similarly, books dealing with developments in the political realm narrated the unfolding of God’s plan for nations and peoples. We therefore shall examine books on the Bible, history, and politics as a single category united in Edwards’ view by providence.**

**of Acts, and a group of Nonconformist ministers prepared the final sixth volume. **Of the three commentators, Edwards’ contemporary Philip Doddridge was the most important for him bibliographically. Leader of a dissenting academy at Northampton, England, Doddridge was a well-known hymn writer whose works attracted a wide audience, even among Anglicans. The detailed marginal notes in Doddridge’s New Testament commentary and paraphrase, the** **Family Expositor** **(6 vols., 1739–56), would prove a gold mine of book leads for Edwards. Doddridge’s commentary first appears in the “Catalogue” in 1738 (no. 405),** **8** **when Edwards notes having received a proposal for printing the work. The following year he obtained the first volume and began mining it for bibliographical information, adding twenty-seven other references to it (and to the later volumes) throughout the “Catalogue.” Among the many books Edwards learned of through Doddridge are several important works on the Bible, including Isaac Newton’s** **Observations upon the Prophecies of Daniel and the Apocalypse of St. John** **(no. 470) and John Mill’s state-of-the-art critical edition of the Greek New Testament (no. 575). Similarly, he learned of several works related to Scripture and the controversy over deism, including the responses to Anthony Collins by Thomas Jeffery (no. 557) and Richard Bentley (no. 569), as well as Nathanael Taylor’s** **Preservative Against Deism** **(no. 561). He also found a reference to the political theorist James Harrington (no. 566), whose** **Commonwealth of Oceana** **(1656), dedicated to Oliver Cromwell, had proposed an elaborate system of checks and balances in government.**

Most recently: **Matthew Henry’s Commentary on the Whole Bible**(Peabody, Mass., Hendrickson Publishers, 1991).

Somewhat similar in aim were texts known as harmonies, which attempted to combine the gospel narratives (and sometimes other sections of Scripture) into a unified narrative. Edwards lists two harmonists in the

**rich Man to get into the Kingdom of Heaven.”** **9** **This old text-critical problem—a few ancient Greek manuscripts read “rope,” a word nearly identical to that for “camel”—was discussed in commentaries of the day, and Fielding apparently assumed his readers’ familiarity with the issue. A fully accurate biblical text was, after all, crucial for establishing the most reliable account of biblical history. Consequently, Edwards eagerly sought resources on textual criticism and translation. In addition to Mill’s** **Novum Testamentum,** **the “Catalogue” also lists in no. 687 the** **Gnomon Novi Testamenti** **(1742), a New Testament commentary by another famous textual scholar, Johann Albrecht Bengel (1687–1752), who drew on his pioneering 1734 critical edition of the New Testament. In addition, the “Catalogue” lists biblical lexicons, concordances, and learned commentaries by Paulus Martinus Alberti (no. 599), Johann Buxtorf the Elder (no. 472), Samuel Clarke (not the philosopher; no. 590), Alexander Cruden (no. 417), Jakob Elsner (no. 567), Henry Hammond (no. 530), Charles-François Houbigant (no. 619), Jean Le Clerc (no. 524), Edward Leigh (no. 44), Christianus Noldius (no. 546), Petrus Ravanellus (no. 418), Johann Scapula (no. 536), Erasmus Schmid (no. 473), and Abraham Trommius (no. 474).** **1** **Two of these works Edwards actually owned: Schmid’s Greek concordance and Buxtorf’s Hebrew concordance, both of which he lent to fellow ministers.**

One curious work on the Bible that Edwards also lent out (and mentioned in “Catalogue,” no. 317) is **A Common-Place Book to the Holy Bible; or, The Scriptures Sufficiency Practically Demonstrated**(1697). Originally issued in 1676 under a variant title and published in five editions before Edwards’ death, this book has often been attributed to John Locke. But the first editor of Locke’s works, Edmund Law (1703–87), bishop of Carlisle, discounted the attribution, and modern scholars have agreed with his assessment. The work in any case must have been appealing to Edwards. Consisting entirely of biblical quotations, it organized them under dozens of theological headings, in effect rearranging key scriptural passages into an orderly systematic theology.

Many moderns would assume a clear distinction between sacred history (as recorded in the Bible and dated by chronologists) and secular history (as recorded by postbiblical historians). But because there was no “secular” history for Edwards, he consumed works on postbiblical history in the same spirit as he read the Bible itself: to discern the hand of providence. The “Account Book” indicates several major historical texts that Edwards owned, including Sir Richard Baker’s **Chronicle of the Kings of England**(1643) and William Howell’s **Institution of General History**(1661), both of which appeared in many later editions, and Robert Millar’s **History of the Propagation of Christianity**(2 vols., 1723). Edwards also owned the **Compleat History of the Turks**(2 vols., 1701) by David Jones, a popular writer who apparently began his career as an English spy in the French court. Meanwhile, the many historical texts in the “Catalogue”

“Catalogue”: the famous Hebraist John Lightfoot (no. 61), a member of the Westminster Assembly, who sought to link the New Testament accounts of Christ with evidence from the Old Testament; and Matthew Pilkington (no. 578), whose **Evangelical History and Harmony,**a synthesis of the gospel accounts, included a list of past harmonists.

**Lightfoot (1602–75) was also known for his attempts to pinpoint the date of the world’s creation. Biblical chronology, based on the traditional assumption that Scripture accurately recorded human history from the Garden of Eden to the close of the apostolic age, was a popular subject in Edwards’ day and one of his lifelong interests. The “Catalogue” lists several significant books on this subject, most famously the** **Annals of the World** **(no. 146) by James Ussher (1581–1656), the Church of Ireland archbishop of Armagh. Ussher, known to posterity for calculating the date of creation as October 23, 4004 b.c.e., is still influential today among conservative Protestant “young earth creationists.” Edwards also mentions Isaac Newton’s** **Chronology of Ancient Kingdoms Amended** **(no. 357), panned by one modern biographer as a “work of colossal tedium.” Newton augmented more traditional accounts by incorporating astronomical proofs as well as evidence from the Egyptians, Assyrians, Babylonians, and other ancients.** **2** **In addition, the “Catalogue” lists Arthur Bedford’s** **Scripture Chronology** **(no. 358) and Henry Winder’s** **Critical and Chronological History** **(no. 475), both of which Edwards later used extensively; as well as William Whiston’s** **Short View of the Chronology of the Old Testament** **(no. 67) and his** **New Theory of the Earth** **(no. 69).**

2. Katz, **God’s Last Words,**101–8, where Robert Westfall is quoted (p. 102) on Newton’s “colossal tedium.”

Finally, there are works dealing in some way with the specter of political Catholicism, which Edwards and other Protestants so feared. Almost all of the political books listed by Edwards are of this type, as are a number of the histories. Many of these books relate to the successive Jacobite plots—at least five in Edwards’ lifetime—to reinstall a Catholic king after

**read like a** **Who’s Who** **of English historians. Here we find the celebrated explorer Sir Walter Raleigh (no. 142), who wrote his uncompleted** **Historie of the World** **(1614) while confined in the Tower of London on treason charges. Later historians reflected the Whig-Tory divide in English politics. Thus Paul de Rapin-Thoyras, a Huguenot who participated in William of Orange’s invasion of England, wrote the Whiggish** **History of England** **(no. 347), which one of Edwards’ fellow ministers commended to him as “the best that Ever was written.” The Tory historian Thomas Salmon responded with his** **Modern History** **(no. 628) praising the Stuart monarchs. In contrast, the Whig pamphleteer John Oldmixon wrote a contentious series of anti-Stuart and anti-Catholic histories, at least one of which Edwards used (no. 221; see also nos. 364 and 385). One of Oldmixon’s targets was the Anglican priest and historian Laurence Echard (nos. 73, 228, and 392), who himself claimed to be of no party but the truth.** **3**

Besides seeking authors who focused on England’s history and politics, Edwards also sought works on other regions and peoples. The “Catalogue” lists histories or travel accounts of Egypt (no. 615), France (no. 525), Greece (nos. 147, 252, 296), Malabar, in present-day Kerala state, India (no. 72), the Netherlands (no. 525), Rome (nos. 73, 627), Scotland (nos. 150, 310, 496, 525), and Spain (no. 525). Histories of the Arabs and the Jews also appear. Edwards mentions the Cambridge Orientalist Simon Ockley’s **History of the Saracens**(no. 665), as well as Ockley’s translation of Leone Modena’s **History of the Present Jews**(no. 137). Similarly, Edwards lists an English translation of Flavius Josephus’ **Wars of the Jews**(no. 445), adding “not Josephus Ben Gorion” to distinguish the first-century Josephus from the medieval Joseph ben Gorion, pseudonymous author of a history of the Jews known as the **Josippon.**Another noteworthy listing is the seven-volume **Universal History**(no. 403), a collection of historical extracts on every country.

Indeed, the sense that “all Protestants” stood in solidarity against the

**the overthrow of James II. After James’ death in 1701, his son James Francis Edward Stuart (the Old Pretender) failed in two Jacobite military expeditions, in 1708 and a more significant effort in 1715. Then, in 1719, the de facto prime minister of Spain, Cardinal Giulio Alberoni, was banished by Spanish king Philip V after his own ill-conceived Jacobite scheme brought disaster on Spain by provoking France, the Netherlands, and the Holy Roman Empire to come to England’s aid. This was followed in 1722 by the bungled Atterbury Plot in England, which implicated the bishop of Rochester, Francis Atterbury. Most disastrous, the Jacobite Rebellion of 1745 (“the Forty-Five”) led by Charles Edward Stuart (“Bonnie Prince Charlie,” the Young Pretender) ended in the wholesale massacre of more than a thousand Jacobites at the Battle of Culloden Moor, Scotland, in 1746.** **4**

**Edwards followed these events closely. We have already seen the series of entries early in the “Catalogue” related to the Atterbury Plot (nos. 175, 176, 178, 180, and 181). Regarding the Cardinal Alberoni debacle, he lists** **A Modest Apology for Parson Alberoni** **(no. 143), an anti-Jacobite satire by the Whig pamphleteer Thomas Gordon, co-editor with John Trenchard of the** **Independent Whig** **(no. 210), a frequently reprinted newspaper attacking the high-church clergy. The stir caused by the Jacobite Rebellion of 1745 is also vividly evident in Edwards’ manuscripts. In “Catalogue,” no. 475, he quotes a newspaper account by Henry Winder, who witnessed the fortification of Liverpool against Jacobite forces. In entry no. 499, he lists Philip Doddridge’s glorified account of the death of a government officer, Col. James Gardiner, in battle against the Jacobite army. In the “Account Book,” Edwards lists four popular anti-Jacobite works: two published a few months before Culloden ( James Burgh’s** **Britain’s Remembrancer,** **and John Willison’s** **Popery, Another Gospel** **), and two published just after the battle (Thomas Prince’s thanksgiving sermon, and George Whitefield’s** **Britain’s Mercies, and Britain’s Duty** **). Edwards commented to Scottish correspondent John MacLaurin that “we, and all Protestants, have great cause of thankfulness; especially all within the British dominions” that the Young Pretender was thwarted by God’s providential intervention.** **5**

Culloden effectively ended the Jacobite threat. See Geoffrey Plank, **Rebellion and Savagery: The Jacobite Rising of 1745 and the British Empire**(Philadelphia, Univ. of Pennsylvania Press, 2006). The best source on fears of Jacobitism in colonial New England is Kidd, **Protestant Interest,**esp. 115–35.

#### Philosophy

**threat of popery is ubiquitous in Edwards’ political and historical reading. Elisha Williams’** **Essential Rights and Liberties of Protestants,** **listed in the “Account Book” and discussed earlier, reflected the typical colonial homage to the Glorious Revolution in referring to “the late great Deliverer (William IIId. of happy Memory) of the British Nation from Popery and Slavery.”** **6** **Not surprisingly, colonial New Englanders also felt a special kinship with the Huguenots, the Protestants (and their descendants) who suffered persecution and exile after Louis XIV revoked the Edict of Nantes in 1685. The earliest entry in the “Account Book” is to the Huguenot minister Andrew le Mercier’s** **Church History of Geneva** **(Boston, 1732). Born André le Mercier (1692–1764), he immigrated from France to America and settled as pastor of the French Church in Boston, where he dedicated his history of Calvin’s city to New England’s ministers.** **7** **Similarly, several Huguenot writers appear in the “Catalogue,” including the theologian Isaac Jaquelot (1647–1708), whose posthumously published** **Specimen of Papal and French Persecution** **(no. 153) was reminiscent of earlier anti-Catholic martyrologies such as John Foxe’s** **Actes and Monuments** **(no. 495) and Samuel Clarke’s (not to be confused with the philosopher)** **Generall Martyrologie** **(no. 349).**

**Yet in reading about past persecutions, Edwards was also anticipating the future as he looked for signs that the papal Antichrist might soon be defeated. On the timing of this event, he differed from the Nonconformist commentator Moses Lowman, whom he first mentions as “Laman” in “Catalogue,” no. 383. After obtaining Lowman’s** **Paraphrase and Notes on the Revelation of St. John** **(1737), Edwards could not accept his conclusion that the papal Antichrist would not be defeated until after the year 2000.** **8** **Christ’s return, Edwards believed, was imminent, and with it the consummation of history.**

**A great deal has been written on Edwards’ relation to the Western philosophical tradition, and this complex question cannot be revisited fully here.** **9** **The “Catalogue” and “Account Book” nevertheless provide**

**some useful evidence of the nature and timing of Edwards’ philosophical interests. The long-unquestioned assumption of his early and decisive intellectual debt to John Locke originated with Samuel Hopkins’ 1765 biography, which claimed that Edwards first read Locke’s** **Essay Concerning Human Understanding** **(1690) in his second year of college, at age thirteen.** **1** **More recently, scholars have suggested that Edwards may have first read Locke’s** **Essay** **as a graduate student or even as a tutor, after the Dummer collection brought the book to New Haven.** **2** **The “Catalogue” letter leaf seems to support this revised hypothesis. In entry no. 15, probably penned in 1724, Edwards lists “Lock of human understanding.” Sometime later, Edwards acquired his own copy of the** **Essay,** **lending it to his son Timothy in 1754, as the “Account Book” reveals. By that point, Edwards had recorded in the “Catalogue” his interest in other philosophical works by Locke, including** **Some Thoughts Concerning Education** **(no. 209),** **A Letter Concerning Toleration** **(no. 219), the one-volume** **Posthumous Works** **(no. 353), and the three-volume** **Works** **(no. 363).**

**The cult of Locke and Newton, as the historian Jonathan Israel has shown, was at the center of a wider Anglomania that swept European philosophy in the eighteenth century.** **3** **That Edwards was caught up in this trend is evident not only from his notations on Locke and Newton themselves but also from his mention of books strongly reflecting their influence. Locke’s ideas in particular—especially on epistemology, logic, and education—are important to Peter Browne’s** **Procedure, Extent, and Limits of Human Understanding** **(no. 652), John Clarke’s** **Essay upon Study** **(no. 315), Jean-Pierre de Crousaz’s** **New Treatise of the Art of Thinking** **(no. 522), William Duncan’s** **Elements of Logick** **(no. 623), David Fordyce’s** **Dialogues Concerning Education** **(no. 598), George Turnbull’s** **Observations upon Liberal Education** **(no. 657), and Isaac Watts’** **Logick** **(no. 313) and** **Improvement of the Mind** **(no. 483).** **4**

Besides seeking works on epistemology and logic, Edwards was an avid reader of moral philosophy. Among the more significant titles in the “Catalogue” is **A Treatise of the Laws of Nature**(no. 335), by Richard Cumberland (1632–1718), bishop of Peterborough, who had earlier gained fame for his study of biblical measures and weights. Elevated to the episcopate by Archbishop Tillotson, Cumberland drew on mathematical terminology to argue that humans are obligated under natural law to promote the common good, which is the only way individual goods can be derived. The “Catalogue” also lists two well-known works of the Ulster-born moral philosopher Francis Hutcheson (1694–1746): his **Inquiry into the Original of Our Ideas of Beauty and Virtue**(no. 410), which articulated the idea of the “moral sense” for perceiving the worth of actions; and his **Essay on the Nature and Conduct of the Passions and Affections**(no.

**At the same time, older philosophical perspectives, especially Cartesianism, are evident in the “Catalogue.” Locke challenged Descartes’ rationalist view that the mind by itself possessed innate ideas, apart from any empirical observation, that could form a reliable basis of knowledge about the world. Though Edwards took Locke’s objections seriously, he was nourished on an early diet of Cartesian rationalism, as contained in such texts as Antoine Arnauld and Pierre Nicole’s** **Art of Thinking** **(no. 16) and William Brattle’s** **Compendium Logicae** **(no. 144).** **5** **Edwards was also aware of the English edition of** **The Search After Truth** **(no. 303) by the French Cartesian Nicolas Malebranche (1638–1715), as well as works by Malebranche’s English followers John Norris (no. 26) and Arthur Collier (no. 664). A onetime disciple of Descartes who later rebelled against Cartesianism was the Dutch mathematician and “physicotheologian” Bernard Nieuwentijt, whose** **Religious Philosopher,** **published in a three-volume English translation in 1718, Edwards lists in “Catalogue,” no. 196.** **6** **Whether Edwards ever actually read Descartes himself is uncertain. He undoubtedly had access: Descartes’** **Works** **and** **Meditations on First Philosophy** **were part of both the Dummer collection and Solomon Stoddard’s library. And as we have seen, Edwards cited Ephraim Chambers’ recommendation of** **Discours de la méthode** **in “Catalogue,” no. 408, though the entry is not crossed out.**

As Bruce Kuklick puts it, “Edwards read Locke in the context of the metaphysical discussion that Descartes dominated”—a discussion still focused on the question of mind and its relationship to God. See Bruce Kuklick, **A History of Philosophy in America, 1720–2000**(Oxford, Clarendon Press, 2001), 10.

On Nieuwentijt see Israel, **Radical Enlightenment,**461, 477–78; on JE and Malebranche, see Fiering, **Jonathan Edwards’s Moral Thought,**40–45.

**The Scottish-born Hume, who undermined traditional metaphysics with his radical empiricism and naturalism, was certainly at odds with Edwards in fundamental ways. Yet Edwards’ eagerness to reckon with Hume and other “corrupt” authors (as expressed in his aforementioned comment to Erskine) distinguished him from many colonial evangelicals of the next generation, who rejected any form of epistemological skepticism out of hand. Early on, Edwards betrayed his interest in “corrupt” philosophy in “Catalogue,” no. 131, which reveals his desire to obtain the** **Essays** **of Montaigne, who famously adopted the motto “Que sais-je?” (What do I know?). (The Dummer collection lacked Montaigne, though outside of New England, William Byrd II owned not one but three sets of the** **Essays.** **)** **1** **Edwards also sought philosophy of a different sort in the**

**552), which explored the problem of self-love in benevolent actions. Edwards later used both these texts in the “Miscellanies.”** **7** **Another text cited in the “Miscellanies” is George Turnbull’s** **Principles of Moral and Christian Philosophy,** **from which Edwards extracted a recommendation of the sermons of Bishop Joseph Butler (“Catalogue,” no. 637). Similarly, the “Catalogue” reveals that Edwards owned or had access to** **A System of Moral Philosophy** **(no. 608), by the Presbyterian schoolmaster Henry Grove.**

**Other significant philosophical works listed in the “Catalogue” include the Newtonian metaphysician Andrew Baxter’s** **Enquiry into the Nature of the Human Soul** **(no. 509), which Edwards later used in** **Freedom of the Will;** **and Henry Home, Lord Kames’ anonymously published** **Essays on Principles of Morality** **(no. 676), which Edwards received from his Scottish correspondent John Erskine.** **8** **From Lord Kames, Edwards gleaned two recommendations of David Hume’s anonymous** **Treatise of Human Nature** **(nos. 676 and 678), which Kames lauded for its “acuteness and penetration” even while disagreeing with some of its basic premises. Edwards seems to have obtained Hume’s treatise soon thereafter, apparently using it in the** **Nature of True Virtue.** **9** **He also obtained Hume’s** **Enquiry Concerning the Principles of Morals,** **from which he copied a glowing recommendation of Montesquieu’s** **De l’esprit des loix** **as “the best system of political Knowledge that perhaps has yet ever been communicated” (no. 682).**

On Cumberland and Hutcheson, see Jon Parkin, “Richard Cumberland,” and James Moore, “Francis Hutcheson,” in **ODNB;**and Fiering, **Jonathan Edwards’s Moral Thought,**77, 129–32.

**works of Bishop Berkeley, whose immaterialism caused many people to regard him—much to his chagrin—as a skeptic.** **2** **The “Catalogue” lists three of Berkeley’s works: his** **Treatise Concerning the Principles of Human Knowledge** **(no. 318), his** **Essay Towards a New Theory of Vision** **(no. 319), and his** **Alciphron; or, The Minute Philosopher** **(no. 350). Wallace Anderson has suggested, moreover, that Edwards used Berkeley’s** **New Theory of Vision** **in “The Mind.”** **3** **Edwards’ interest in Berkeley contrasts strikingly with the hostility toward the bishop-philosopher among later evangelicals like John Witherspoon, the Scottish divine who became president of Princeton a decade after Edwards’ death. Influenced by the Common Sense Realism of Thomas Reid (1710–96), Witherspoon refused to take Berkeley’s immaterialism seriously, once reputedly remarking that a student who swallowed a hot drink too quickly was burned by the “idea” of hot toddy. Witherspoon also derided the “infidel” Hume for “shak[ing] the certainty of our belief upon cause and effect,” and sought to purge the College of New Jersey of Hume and Berkeley’s influence.** **4** **Little did Witherspoon know of the “Catalogue” entries on Hume and Berkeley, which reveal Edwards’ recognition of these two philosophers’ importance.**

Science in Edwards’ day was still called natural philosophy and it covered the entire gamut of scientific fields, from astronomy and meteorology to anatomy and botany. Whereas science today is marked by clear disciplinary boundaries, science in colonial America was undifferentiated

Yale president Thomas Clap, who died a year before Witherspoon became president of Princeton in 1768, waged a similar campaign to keep the college free of unorthodox influence. When a Baptist merchant in Newport, R.I., offered Yale a donation in 1759 on the condition that all books (whether orthodox or not) “be available to students,” Clap refused the gift over the objection of Newport minister and future Yale president Ezra Stiles (see David D. Insofar as Clap and Stiles represented two competing visions of learned culture, JE was caught in the middle; still fully committed to Reformed orthodoxy, he nevertheless sought access to the full range of Enlightenment thought.

**By Edwards’ day, membership in the Royal Society was a considerable honor. Only a handful of colonials had been inducted, beginning with the Connecticut Governor John Winthrop, Jr. The young Edwards undoubtedly daydreamed about the prestige of appending “F.R.S.” (Fellow of the Royal Society) to his own name.** **7** **Through Paul Dudley, a fellow of the society and Massachusetts judge, Edwards sought to have his “Spider Letter” of October 1723 published in the society’s organ,** **Philosophical Transactions,** **but the manuscript was never printed. The “Catalogue” nevertheless reveals Edwards’ ongoing interest in the society’s activities.**

**by field and unsupported by academic infrastructure. “The entire corpus of natural philosophy,” notes the historian Raymond Phineas Stearns, “was still within the capacities of a single scholar.”** **5** **Edwards was such a scholar. Throughout his life he sought learned treatises on scientific topics as well as books on the mathematics necessary for scientific inquiry. The final entry in the “Catalogue” (no. 720), penned just a few months before his death, lists not a work of divinity but a treatise on geometry by a French Jesuit. For Edwards, every mathematical theorem or scientific discovery revealed God’s providential design.**

**This providential attitude toward science had nevertheless changed with the rise of mechanical philosophy in the latter half of the seventeenth century. The world was now widely regarded as being subject to divinely instituted natural laws, which God rarely violated. When England’s first scientific guild, the Royal Society, was founded in 1660, its members agreed to subject all scientific conclusions to “mature debate & clear arguments, chiefly such as are deduced from legitimate experiments.” Gone were the days when strange occurrences in nature were automatically assumed to be special providences, or arbitrary divine interventions. The society would eschew the enthusiastic providentialism of the Commonwealth era, or as the society’s historian Thomas Sprat put it, “the Artifice, and Humors, and Passions of Sects.”** **6**

**A number of prominent scientists and mathematicians are listed in the “Catalogue.” Isaac Newton is of course ubiquitous: his** **Principia** **and** **Opticks** **(nos. 63, 194) appear, along with works about his discoveries by Willem Jacob ’s-Gravesande (no. 311), Colin MacLaurin (no. 491), Benjamin Martin (no. 604), Henry Pemberton (no. 334), Jacques Rohault (no. 70), and William Whiston (no. 215). Mathematicians in the “Catalogue” include Louis-Bertrand Castel (no. 423), Jacques Ozanam (no. 90), Ignace Gaston Pardies (no. 720), and André Tacquet (no. 246). Edwards also lists natural histories by John Woodward (no. 99), Noël Antoine Pluche (no. 594), and John Hill (no. 622). Woodward, who carried on an extensive correspondence with Cotton Mather, sought to demonstrate in his** **Natural History of the Earth** **that the fossil remains he had collected were those of creatures destroyed by the biblical flood.** **8**

**Astronomy held special interest for Edwards, who once wrote that the “late invention of telescopes, whereby heavenly objects are brought so much nearer . . . is a type and forerunner of the great increase in knowledge of heavenly things that shall be in the approaching glorious times of the Christian church.”** **9** **During his Yale tutorship, he listed in the “Catalogue” the manuscript astronomical lectures of fellow tutor Robert Treat (no. 68), who published an almanac of celestial motions and events. Around the same time Edwards listed the** **Kosmotheoros** **(no. 289) of the famous Dutch scientist Christiaan Huygens (1629–95), who privately had echoed his rival Baruch Spinoza in denying the possibility of miracles in a universe governed by natural laws.** **1** **A more conventionally religious astronomer was the Cambridge don and Anglican divine Roger Long, whose** **Astronomy** **(no. 422) Edwards learned of in advance from the** **Republick of Letters.** **Edwards also listed a popular text on astronomy and geography by Isaac Watts (no. 314), who took as the book’s epigraph Psalm 8:3 (“I consider thy heavens, the work of thy fingers”).**
