**Yet for all the evidence of the new science in Edwards’ reading, we also find texts that betray the lingering medieval assumptions of Edwards’ world. This is especially true of books related to biology and the human body. Early in the “Catalogue,” for example, Edwards lists “Van helmonts Philosophy” (no. 75), namely, the anatomical and other works of Jean Baptiste van Helmont (1577–1644), a Flemish physician and chemist. Though he laid the groundwork for the modern classification of diseases and also pioneered pneumatic science (the study of gases), Van Helmont was a famous dabbler in medieval mysticism and alchemy.** **3** **A more upto-date text of anatomy, William Cowper’s** **Anatomy of Humane Bodies** **(1698; 2nd ed., 1737), also appears in the “Catalogue” (no. 100), but this work too reveals its close proximity to the medieval past when it notes the only recent acceptance of the theory that human reproduction occurs through egg and sperm rather than through the comingling of essentially identical male and female “seeds.”** **4**

**Of all the titles listed in the “Catalogue,” the lone book on a frankly sexual topic mixed quasi-medical description with stern warnings about biblical taboos. The title of the anonymous** **Onania; or, The Heinous Sin of Self-Pollution** **(no. 276) recalls the fate of the biblical Onan, whom God smote for spilling his seed on the ground (Genesis 38:9–10). This anti-masturbation treatise appeared in at least nineteen editions, including one printed in Boston in 1724, around the time Edwards listed the book in the “Catalogue.”** **Onania** **used the familiar epistolary style to detail the afflictions allegedly caused by masturbation, from back pain and red spots on the skin to mental impairment and wholesale bodily decline. Billed as advice for “both sexes,” the text concluded with a cautionary letter to married couples against “gratify[ing] their Lust” through the “abominable Sin” of coitus interruptus, which frustrated the procreative purpose of intercourse. For persons who had already committed this offense or the sin of masturbation,** **Onania** **insisted that a sense of grief and repentance “should remain with them to their Lives end.”** **7**

This and Thomas Dawkes’** **Midwife Rightly Instructed** **(1736) were the infamous “Bad Books” circulated by several boys in Edwards’ Northampton congregation.** **5** **Edwards mentions neither in the “Catalogue,” though he does list another midwifery manual by the man-midwife Edmund Chapman (no. 424), who, like Dawkes, was critical of female midwives for holding “too great an Opinion of their own Judgment.” Chapman wrote his treatise especially for female midwives, adapting it “to their Capacities” and employing delicate language that could be read “without Blushes.” He included no illustrations or diagrams since these might “raise impure Thoughts and Ideas in the Reader’s Mind.”** **6** **Yet as the Bad Book case proved, inexpensive chapbooks on medical topics—popular alternatives to an elite medical literature still in Latin—could easily be used for sexual titillation.**

#### Books by Female Authors

**Whereas lifelong repentance was the only sure remedy for masturbatory maladies, a variety of nonsexual ailments found cures in an eccentric handbook,** **An Authentic Narrative of the Success of Tar-Water** **(1746), the only text resembling a scientific work in Edwards’ “Account Book.” Printed in Dublin, London, and Boston, this popular manual was by Thomas Prior, a founder of the Royal Dublin Society and a friend of the philosopher George Berkeley, who first helped popularize the use of cold water infused with tar as a remedy for a wide variety of bodily afflictions. Berkeley learned of the use of tar water during his 1729–31 sojourn in Rhode Island, where he briefly contemplated establishing an Anglican college after the failure of a similar scheme for a college in Bermuda.** **8** **At that time, the American colonies produced much of the tar and pitch used in Britain, and Berkeley came to regard tar water as a general panacea, advocating it even as a drink for infants. His own opinions on the subject appeared in** **Siris** **(1744), which not surprisingly would prompt some critics to wonder how an immaterialist could coherently speak of physical causes and effects. Berkeley did not miss a beat, insisting in the book that “all phaenomena are, to speak truly, appearances in the soul or mind; it hath never been explained, nor can it be explained, how external bodies, figures, and motions should produce an appearance in the mind.”** **9**

At least seven women appear among the hundreds of authors listed in the “Catalogue” and “Account Book,” though because female writers in the eighteenth century often published anonymously or pseudonymously, their full contributions to Edwards’ reading world may never be known. Indeed, three of the seven women—Eliza Haywood, Mary Astell, and Susanna Newcome—appear anonymously, and Edwards probably never learned of their names. The most notable of these is Eliza Haywood (1693?–1756), whose periodical the **Female Spectator**Edwards lists in “Catalogue,” no. 592. Best known for her novel **The History of Miss Betsy Thoughtless**(1751), along with more than fifty other fictional works, Haywood was a controversial figure whose narratives of seduction and intrigue

Berkeley’s hopes for an “Episcopal Seminary in Rhode Island” quickly faded when he realized the legal difficulties of amending the charter for his failed Bermuda scheme; see Gaustad, **George Berkeley in America,**129–33.

**Mary Astell (1666–1731), by contrast, demonstrably influenced Edwards. Unbeknown to him, she was the original source of the rules for writing that he as a young man had resolved to follow. The rules appeared without attribution in the most popular of early eighteenth-century conduct books,** **The Ladies Library,** **which scholars have shown was compiled by Bishop Berkeley.** **3** **Astell was a keen student of philosophy who carried on a lengthy correspondence with the Cambridge Platonist John Norris. An early champion of female education, she argued in an anonymously published work,** **A Serious Proposal to the Ladies** **(1694), that secular convents should be established where women could freely pursue philosophy, theology, and the wider life of the mind. In a second part of** **A Serious Proposal** **(1697) dedicated to her admirer, the future queen Anne, Astell included a chapter on the “Improvement of the Understanding,” in which she laid out epistemological and logical principles influenced by the Port-Royal school. This section included the six rules for writing, which counseled economy of expression (“Cut off all needless Ideas”) even while urging examination of all facets of an issue. “We may stop short of Truth as well as over-run it,” she explained, if we fail to examine a problem from multiple angles.** **4** **As a succinct guide to logical**

**pushed the boundaries of eighteenth-century literary convention. She was also a clever satirist whose** **Anti-Pamela; or, Feigned Innocence Detected** **(1741) lampooned Samuel Richardson’s virtuous heroine.** **1** **The anonymously issued** **Female Spectator,** **first published monthly between 1744 and 1746 and subsequently in several bound editions, addressed female readers on a wide variety of topics, from dealing with unfaithful husbands to learning about the natural world through observation.** **2** **Though it is likely Edwards never obtained Haywood’s literary periodical—the entry for it in the “Catalogue” is not crossed out—it was clearly a genre he appreciated.**

Fearing misrepresentation by her enemies, Haywood apparently enjoined close acquaintances to not share details of her life, which has made biographical reconstruction difficult; see Christine Blouch, “Eliza Haywood and the Romance of Obscurity,” **Studies in English Literature, 1500–1900**31 (1991), 535–52, esp. 545.

The other female authors in the “Catalogue” and “Account Book” appear by name and were writers of a more devotional bent. The most famous was the evangelical poet Elizabeth Singer Rowe (1674–1737), who appears three times in the “Catalogue” (nos. 190, 406, and 433). Daughter

**argumentation, the rules quickly gained a following. Richard Steele, who had once mocked Astell as the leader of “an order of Platonick Ladies,” gave the rules his tacit imprimatur when he published them in** **The Ladies Library** **and wrote the book’s preface on behalf of Berkeley as the anonymous compiler.** **5** **Meanwhile, Edwards, as we have seen, lent out** **The Ladies Library** **more than any other book, thereby conferring his own unwitting approval of Astell as a philosophical and logical thinker.**

**Another philosophically inclined female writer was Susanna Newcome, whom the English Short Title Catalogue identifies as the author of** **An Enquiry into the Evidence of the Christian Religion,** **listed by Edwards in “Catalogue,” no. 359. No details of Newcome’s life have been located, but her book, published simultaneously in Cambridge and London in 1728, with an expanded London edition in 1732, garnered a notice in the** **Republick of Letters,** **which brought the work to Edwards’ attention. An attempt to demonstrate the reasonableness of Christianity, Newcome’s book sounded a Lockean note in describing the initial state of the human mind as “empty and void, without any innate Ideas,” until knowledge is obtained through “Ideas of Sensation.” “And as there are no innate Ideas of God,” Newcome concluded, “so likewise we can have no Proof of such a Being** **a priori.** **” We can only know God through observation of things in nature, which exist because of a chain of causation originating with the First Cause. As for Jesus, Newcome echoed Locke’s** **Reasonableness of Christianity** **in arguing that the miracles worked by him and the prophecies fulfilled in him proved that he was the Messiah and confirmed the divine status of the Christian revelation. She attacked the deist Matthew Tindal’s** **Christianity as Old as the Creation** **for presuming that no such divine revelation was necessary.** **6** **All told, Newcome’s book, in both its subject matter and its anonymous guise, anticipated attempts a century later by such American women as Catharine Beecher to enter the male-dominated sphere of philosophical and theological debate.** **7**

**Gilberte Pascal Périer (1620–85) was the sister and biographer of the famous mathematician and philosopher Blaise Pascal. **Like La Musse’s** **Triumphs of Grace,** **Hannah Housman’s** **Power and Pleasure of the Divine Life** **(1744; “Catalogue,” no. 662) depicted the unwavering faith of the author during her final illness. Housman (d. 1735) was the sister of Richard Pearsall, an Independent minister in England, who compiled the book from her diary and added an account of her death. He successfully promoted his sister’s work through his network of evangelical contacts, including Philip Doddridge, George Whitefield, and James Hervey.** **3** **A Boston edition appeared in 1755, and Edwards obtained the volume soon thereafter, as the “Account Book” reveals. The Jansenism of the Pascal family undoubtedly increased the appeal of their writings for Edwards, who, as we have seen, considered Jansenist texts to be among the few Catholic sources not utterly awash in error.

**The remaining two works by women resemble the** **Life** **of Pascal in recounting the “beautiful death” of a pious person.** **1** **The two posthumously published volumes each consisted of the author’s sayings, redacted by her acquaintances and embellished with an account of her final hours. The first book was by Margaret (Marguerite) de la Musse (1664?–81), a Huguenot born to a noble French family, who died at age sixteen following an unspecified illness. The transatlantic popularity of her** **Triumphs of Grace; or, The Last Words and Edifying Death of the Lady Margaret de la Musse** **(1687; “Catalogue,” no. 36) is evident from a Boston edition published in 1717. Reminiscent of Mary Rowlandson’s captivity narrative of 1682 in its frequent allusions to biblical verses,** **Triumphs of Grace** **notes that La Musse “took great delight in the paraphrasing of the Scripture; seeming, as it were, to have receiv’d a new Vocation from God” to edify others with scriptural providences. Her final moment was no exception as she uttered the** **Nunc Dimittis** **(Luke 2:29): “Lord, now lettest thou thy servant depart in peace, according to thy Word.”** **2**

**No taxonomy can do justice to the full range of texts in the “Catalogue” and “Account Book,” but several remaining genres and subjects deserve mention. Grammars, dictionaries, and related works on language constitute a significant category. A notable title here is Mathurin Cordier’s** **Colloquies,** **which the “Account Book” reveals that Edwards owned. Cordier (“Corderius”) was John Calvin’s own Latin instructor and later a teacher in the Geneva Academy. He insisted, somewhat quixotically, that young boys should be able to converse easily in Latin with their mothers.** **6** **His** **Colloquies,** **a series of Latin readings, appeared with a literal English translation in many editions, including one at Boston in 1724. The “Catalogue,” meanwhile, shows Edwards’ interest in more upto-date Latin texts, including the** **New Grammar of the Latin Tongue** **(nos. 498 and 540), by the English schoolmaster John Clarke. Similarly, the “Catalogue” lists several English grammars, including that of James Greenwood (1683?–1737). First published in 1711 and reprinted at least five times in Edwards’ day, Greenwood’s** **Essay Towards a Practical English Grammar** **(also listed in the “Account Book”) borrowed extensively from John Locke, often without attribution. Greenwood advocated a pedagogy opposite to Cordier’s, insisting that children be taught the grammar of their native language before being schooled in Latin.** **7** **The “Catalogue” also lists several English dictionaries, including John Minsheu’s** **Guide into Tongues** **(no. 17), which compiled etymological evidence from ten other languages; Nathan Bailey’s** **Dictionarium Britan**

Finally, notice should be made of several religious texts that fall outside the categories of Christian divinity books discussed earlier. Edwards’ direct acquaintance with non-Christian sources was limited, though as we have seen he eagerly sought secondary works on world religions. The only primary source on Islam listed in the “Catalogue” is George Sale’s 1734 edition of the Qur’an (no. 420), the first translation directly from the Arabic into English. The Dummer collection included an earlier English translation of the Qur’an derived from a French edition; Edwards may have seen this in New Haven even if he never acquired the Sale translation. Jewish texts, meanwhile, are slightly more numerous in the “Catalogue.” Earlier, we saw several “Catalogue” entries—to the Talmud (no. 264), Philo (no. 267), and Maimonides (no. 268)—made by Edwards at the beginning of his Yale tutorship, just after his experience in New York City with a Jewish neighbor. The same stretch of entries also includes a reference to “the Chaldee Paraphrast” (no. 266)—that is, the Targums, the ancient Aramaic interpretive translations of the Hebrew Bible (“Chaldee” is an obsolete term for Aramaic). Many of the early followers of Jesus were familiar with the Targums, which consequently attracted

**the religious sublime” that also included Blackmore, Rowe, and Watts, among others. For evangelicals, this poetical canon’s value lay in its use of lively images to spur religious conversion.** **3**

**Perhaps owing to a residual Puritan distrust of the theater, Edwards seems to have had little interest in drama. Shakespeare is nowhere to be found—a notable contrast with William Byrd II’s library, which included a folio edition of the Bard’s plays.** **4** **The only dramatic work listed in the “Catalogue” is Joseph Addison’s** **Cato** **(no. 65), which recounted the famous Roman statesman’s suicide to avoid submitting to Julius Caesar’s tyranny. Though Addison endeavored to avoid offending either Whig or Tory in the play, in America** **Cato** **would eventually become the favorite of such revolutionaries as Benjamin Franklin and George Washington, who revered it as a statement of human liberty and republican virtue. Washington even had the play performed by his able-bodied soldiers during the hard winter at Valley Forge in 1777–78.** **5** **Whether Edwards ever obtained the book, much less foresaw its revolutionary implications, is unknown.**

**Christian interest in the language of Jewish Scripture is evident in a different way in “Catalogue,” no. 601, where Edwards lists “Hutchinson on the Hebrew language,” a reference to John Hutchinson (1674– 1737), author of the two-volume** **Moses’s Principia** **(1724–27) and other works. Claiming to have found hidden messages in scriptural Hebrew, Hutchinson argued that the very letters of the Old Testament were divinely inspired and that the vowel points (diacritical marks inserted later to aid in vocalization of the all-consonantal alphabet) were a Jewish perversion of the text’s original meaning. Though Hutchinson was later ridiculed by Leslie Stephen as a “half-educated and fanciful man of boundless vanity,” his peculiar brand of Christian Kabbalism inspired a considerable following of “Hutchinsonians” in eighteenth-century England and the colonies.** **6** **One of the most prominent colonial disciples was Samuel Johnson, who by 1757 was emphasizing Hebrew instruction at New York’s infant King’s College so that students might decipher the Bible’s hidden meanings.** **7** **The “Catalogue,” meanwhile, reveals that Edwards learned of Hutchinson from Thomas Prince in late 1751 or early 1752. That Edwards was a part of this wave of Hutchinsonian fascination is not surprising, given his attraction to the idea of a prisca theologia first revealed in the Hebrew Bible and later reflected in the wisdom of the pagan philosophers. As Theophilus Gale put it in the preface to the** **Court of the Gentiles,** **“all knowledge is from the Hebrew.”** **8** **Edwards’ eagerness to unlock esoteric meanings in the Book of Books also serves as a fitting conclusion to our survey of his extraordinary career as a reader.**

In many ways, the “Catalogue” and “Account Book” are the most problem-laden manuscripts in the Jonathan Edwards Collection at the Beinecke Library at Yale. Edwards’ fragmentary book references present the most obvious challenge, and annotating them has been the first priority of this volume. The preceding sections of this introduction have painted a composite picture of Edwards’ myriad book entries in order to open a new window into both his own intellectual development and the wider

Whereas horizontal strikethroughs (re-created typographically in this volume) abound on the letter leaf, vertical strikethroughs (indicated here with a dagger symbol, †) begin on page 1 of the manuscript proper. Indeed, all the entries on page 1 (nos. 183–239) are crossed out vertically. The horizontal strikethroughs end by page 4, except where Edwards indicates a textual deletion within an entry. The vertical strikethroughs continue to the end of the manuscript, gradually becoming more sporadic, with some pages containing none at all. Whether these markings indicate books that Edwards actually read can be proven only if he cites a volume elsewhere in his manuscripts. Many of the crossed-out entries do in fact list books we know he used, while most of the entries not crossed out appear to be books not cited elsewhere in his manuscripts. Moreover, his cross-referencing of entries in the “Catalogue” proper suggests that he kept an ongoing tally of his actual reading. It therefore appears likely that the vertical strikethroughs in the “Catalogue” proper do indeed indicate books Edwards actually read.

circulation of ideas in colonial British America. We now turn to the more technical manuscript issues surrounding Edwards’ reading documents. One issue is his enigmatic use of strikethroughs and marginal symbols in the “Catalogue.” Another is dating, especially in the “Catalogue,” where most of the entries lack any clue as to when they were written. A third problem is missing manuscript leaves in the “Account Book,” which has five significant lacunae.

**A quick visual inspection of the “Catalogue” (both the letter leaf and the forty-three numbered pages of the manuscript proper) reveals that many of the entries are crossed out with either horizontal or vertical lines or both. To the left of some entries is also an X-mark or asterisk (*). “No amount of study makes these markings clear,” confessed the literary historian Thomas H. Johnson in 1931. He speculated that the strikethroughs, at least, indicated books Edwards had actually read, but he admitted that this was not an ironclad rule.** **9** **Indeed, on the letter leaf in particular, one need not search long before encountering entries not crossed out that list books we know Edwards read and even owned—for example, Locke’s** **Essay Concerning Human Understanding** **(no. 15) and Arnauld and Nicole’s** **Art of Thinking** **(no. 16).** **1**

Apart from ink and paper analysis, the other method of dating “Catalogue” entries is from bibliographical and other clues provided within. Unfortunately, the letter leaf is largely lacking in such evidence, though one entry—a reference to Edwards’ fellow Yale tutor Robert Treat in no. 71—supports Schafer’s theory that the letter leaf dates from 1724. Beginning with the entries of the “Catalogue” proper (nos. 183ff), however, a number of references to books, newspapers, or personal corre

various manuscripts, Thomas A. Schafer noticed that all or most of the Xs and asterisks after page 4 of the “Catalogue” are in bluish-black modern ink, evidently the work of a later user or owner of the manuscript. Nevertheless, Edwards did apparently initiate the system of Xs and asterisks himself, beginning with no. 183, the first entry of the “Catalogue” proper, which is marked with an X. One early listing—of the **Guardian**in no. 191—is marked with three Xs. Edwards also made asterisks to the left of certain entries (for example, no. 262, Richard Steele’s **Churchill’s Annals**), though many asterisks simply signal a cross-reference. Edwards’ own asterisks, save for those preceding cross-references, are reproduced here typographically (*), whereas entries marked with an X are indicated by a pound sign (#) following the entry number.

**A different problem is the dating of “Catalogue” entries, which is of particular significance for scholars interested in Edwards’ intellectual development. Here again, Thomas Schafer’s analysis must be taken into account. Judging from watermark and ink similarities between Edwards’ early sermons and the first page of the “Catalogue” proper, Schafer concluded that Edwards must have begun the manuscript in the New York period, in late 1722.** **2** **He further suggested that Edwards began the letter leaf later, after arriving in New Haven for his tutorship in June 1724, when he would have spent several weeks browsing the college library. One possible indication of this is the address on the letter leaf, written in Timothy Edwards’ handwriting (“To Mr. Jonathan Edwards At Yale Colledge In New Haven”), though Yale had already been consolidated in New Haven by Edwards’ senior undergraduate year. But Schafer also noticed that the ink near the bottom of the first column of letter leaf entries matches that used for “Miscellanies,” no. 126, which he dated from 1724.** **3** **The letter leaf was therefore probably begun after the “Catalogue” proper (see the summary of Schafer’s conjectures in table 1). Nevertheless, for the sake of editorial simplicity and in keeping with the Yale Edition’s original numbering system, Edwards’ entries are numbered sequentially in this volume, beginning with those of the letter leaf.**

**In the “Account Book,” meanwhile, the problem is not chronology— most of the entries are dated—but manuscript lacunae. This small notebook of seventy-four numbered pages has five gaps: pp. 9–26 (except for extant fragments), 29–32, 39–46, 49–52, and 57–58. Any final quantitative judgments about Edwards’ lifelong book-lending patterns must therefore remain provisional since missing leaves may yet surface. Indeed, as this volume was being prepared for press, a missing leaf (pp. 69–70) was found tipped into a copy of Jonathan Edwards Wood-bridge,** **The Memorial Volume of the Edwards Family Meeting at Stockbridge, Mass., September 6–7, A.D. 1870** **(Boston, 1871), at the Huntington Library in San Marino, California.** **5** **This missing page contained more than a dozen additional book references, which have been included here. Other fragments, either from the “Account Book” or separate record sheets, were previously located at the Hartford Seminary Library in Hartford, Connecticut, and the Forbes Library in Northampton, Massachusetts.** **6** **Book transactions listed on these documents have also been included in this volume.**

Edwards’ own page-number citations from books and periodicals are generally not annotated. In most cases, unless otherwise noted, these are references (often culled from marginal notes) to other book titles. In “Catalogue,” no. 707, for example, Edwards lists more than forty page numbers from Christoph Matthäus Pfaff’s **Institutiones Theologiae Dogmaticae**where Pfaff cites Hermann Witsius’ **De Oeconomia Foederum.**Annotating such citations would prove cumbersome and be unnecessary for most readers.

Where the place of a book’s publication is listed on the title page in its old Latin form, the modern English equivalent has been substituted. Thus, for example, “Lugduni Batauorum” is given as “Leiden,” and “Tiguri” is listed as “Zurich.”

The “Account Book” requires a somewhat different editorial format. Because only its book entries are included here, and because Edwards often lent out the same book on more than one occasion, the annotated book references, alphabetized by author name, are listed first, followed by a verbatim listing of each entry in which the book appears. Each verbatim entry is preceded by the manuscript page number (enclosed in square brackets) where the notation occurs. In cases where Edwards does not give a date for the book-lending transaction, the approximate date— inferred from surrounding dated entries—is supplied in square brackets. Information not relevant to the book reference in question is omitted and indicated by bracketed ellipses.

The book entries in this volume appear **verbatim ac literatim**as Edwards wrote them. Previous volumes in the Yale Edition have published his works in edited form, but the uniqueness of the “Catalogue” and “Account Book” requires a documentary format that presents Edwards’ fragmentary book references—including those not positively identifiable —in all their complexity. This verbatim presentation nevertheless introduces a difficulty that was less of an issue in previous volumes: faithfully transcribing Edwards’ erratic capitalization. Not only did he fail to adhere to any systematic capitalization practices, his uppercase letters are often barely distinguishable from lowercase in size, making certain let-ters—such as “C” and “c,” “M” and “m”—very difficult to tell apart. Another recurring problem is his “d,” which he almost always wrote in the lowercase style, with an ascender curling to the left. Whether he intended any of these “d’s” to be uppercase is not clear, but they are transcribed here as they appear, often resulting in lowercased proper names and titles (for example, “dr.”).

In the “Catalogue,” editorial insertions and substitutions are enclosed in square brackets ([ ]). These include entry numbers, which Edwards did not supply, and cross-references, which have been converted from his own symbol system to bracketed entry numbers preceded by a section sign (§). Only two of Edwards’ symbols appear here, “X” for “Christ,” and “ ” for “world.” Edwards’ own textual insertions are indicated with angle brackets (< >). Most of these are instances where he returned to old entries, sometimes years later, to add additional book information or insert a cross-reference. Manuscript page breaks within “Catalogue” entries, meanwhile, are indicated with an asterisk enclosed in square brackets ([*]), followed by an asterisk at the relevant page number indication (for example, *[**Page 6, column 1**]).

**Finally, a few editorial decisions related to annotations should be explained. Because the capitalization of book titles was not yet standardized in the eighteenth century—a printed title often included all-capital portions as well several different sizes of capital letters—titles here are given in the “down style” preferred by libraries and described in** **Anglo-American Cataloguing Rules.** **8** **Thus, the only title words normally capitalized in annotations are proper names and the first word of the title or an alternate title. (The first words of subtitles preceded by a colon are not capitalized, though here subjective judgments are inevitable because of the lack of punctuation on many title pages.) In a few cases, if another book title is quoted within a title, the first word of the quoted title is capitalized.**

For early American book titles, the Evans number (based on the American Bibliography by Charles Evans) is furnished. Identification numbers from the **English Short Title Catalogue**and the Online Computer Library Center (OCLC) have not been supplied because of the frequent uncertainty, particularly in the case of oft-reprinted books, about which edition Edwards had in mind. Usually, the first edition of a book is listed, unless compelling information is available about an edition Edwards owned or used. Researchers interested in full technical information about editions can find most titles either on OCLC Worldcat or on Copac, the unified catalogue of the Consortium of Research Libraries, which includes major book repositories in the United Kingdom and Ireland.

[1.] Bible Edwards used the English Bible, chiefly the Authorized or King James Version (1611), for most of his exegesis. His “Blank Bible,” the largest repository of his biblical commentary, is a duodecimo King James edition (London, 1652) interleaved with 902 quarto manuscript pages of commentary (MS in the Beinecke Rare Book and Manuscript Library, Yale University). For study in the original biblical languages, Edwards used a polyglot Bible with the Old Testament in Hebrew, the Apocrypha and New Testament in Greek, and the whole interlined in Latin: **Biblia Hebraica: eorundem Latina interpretatio Xantis Pagnini Lucensis, Benedicti Ariae Montani ...**(Geneva, 1609), bound with **Novum Testamentum Graecum, cum vulgata interpretatione Latina Graeci contextus lineis inserta . . .**(Geneva, 1609). Edwards’ copy (inscribed “Jonathan Edwards’ Book. 1751,” not the date he acquired it but the date he moved to Stockbridge) is in the Firestone Library, Princeton University (see Appendix C). He also purchased English Bibles (presumably the King James Version) for resale to his parishioners; the Account Book records more than a dozen such transactions, including the sale of “great” Bibles for £6, 5**s,**and “small” Bibles for £1, 10**s.**Finally, according to Sereno Dwight, Edwards had a Bible in which he recorded birth, marriage, and death dates of his family members; this Bible is no longer extant, but the geneaological information was printed by Dwight in **The Works of President Edwards**(10 vols. New York, 1830), **1,**762.

[2.] Mr. Baxters life Richard Baxter (1615–91), famous Nonconformist divine, **Reliquiae Baxterianae; or, Mr. Richard Baxters narrative of the most memorable passages of his life and times: faithfully publish’d from his own original manuscript by Matthew Sylvester**(London, 1696). The Dummer

Collection included Edmund Calamy (1671–1732), **An abridgment of Mr. Baxter’s History of his life and times: with an account of many others of those worthy ministers who were ejected after the restauration of King Charles the Second**. . . (see no. 81).

[4.] His manuscripts Solomon Stoddard (1643–1729). Edwards, as Stoddard’s successor at Northampton, had access to his grandfather’s papers. The extant manuscripts are scattered in several collections, including the Burke Library, Union Theological Seminary (New York); the American Antiquarian Society (Worcester, Massachusetts); and the Massachusetts Historical Society (Boston).

The contributors to the** **Guardian** **included the philosopher George Berkeley (1685– 1753), and in a more limited way, the poet and essayist Alexander Pope (1688–1744), despite his Tory political leanings. The** **Guardian** **served as the Whig rival to the Tory** **Examiner,** **though the** **Guardian** **’s fictitious Nestor Ironside declared himself “as regards the government of the Church, a Tory; with respect to the State, a Whig.”** **1** **The Guardian also included extracts from other authors, including the late archbishop of Canterbury,John Tillot** **son (1630–1694).**

A sermon preach’d before the king, at the royal chapel at St. James’, on Sunday March 31, 1717**(London, 1717), in “Miscellanies,” no. 68 (**Works, 13,**236–37), written in the same period as this “Catalogue” entry. Hoadly donated three of his own works to the Dummer Collection: **The reasonableness of conformity to the Church of England**..., 2nd ed. **[38.] Luthers Colloquies Martin Luther (1483–1546),** **Dris Martini Lutheri colloquia mensalia; or, Dr. Martin Luther’s divine discourses at his table . . . containing questions and answers touching religion, and many other main points of doctrine, as also many notable histories, and all sorts of learning, comforts, advises, prophesies, admonitions, directions and instructions,** **trans. Henry Bell (London, 1652). This was the first edition (abridged) of Luther’s “Table Talk” (** **Tischreden** **) in English. Bell was a sea captain who claimed in the book’s introduction that he had been instructed to translate the** **Tischreden** **by an “antient man,” arrayed in white, who visited him in the middle of the night. Bell’s edition removed or altered some of Luther’s most explicit defenses of the doctrine of the Real Presence in the Eucharist— apparently in order to secure approval of the book by the Rump Parliament.** **3**

**[173.] forbid sabbath breech Reference uncertain. Edwards may be referring to one of the many Sabbatarian tracts published in Stuart England. Puritan Sabbatarianism was especially aroused by the** **Book of Sports** **(issued by James I in 1618 and reissued by Charles I in 1633), which allowed a number of recreations on Sunday. The Puritan Sabbath was enforced during Cromwell’s Protectorate, when even going for a walk on Sunday became a crime.** **1**

(London, 1679).

**[177.] king** hi **Exhortation to the Ecclesiastical Cantons not to persecute Meaning uncertain. Possibly a reference to an appeal by George I (1714–27) to the Protestant cantons in Switzerland to abrogate the requirement that all clergy subscribe to the Helvetic Consensus (1675), a statement of high Reformed orthodoxy. The king issued the appeal following a similar entreaty to the cantons by William Wake (1716–1737), archbishop of Canterbury, who had been prevailed upon by the Genevan theologian Jean-Alphonse Turrettini (1671–1737). The consensus was abrogated in most of the Protestant regions of Switzerland by 1725 (cf. “Jean Alphonse Turrettini” in** **NSH** **).** **2**

**[180.] Dr friend Member of Parliament Confined to his Own house for high treason John Freind (1675–1728), a London physician, member of Parliament, and advocate of smallpox inoculation. As a young man, Freind became friends with Francis Atterbury, the future Jacobite conspirator (see no. 176). In 1723, after it was revealed that Freind had paid for a nurse for the newly born Young Pretender in the exiled Stuart court in Rome, he was imprisoned in the Tower of London for three months on the suspicion he had used the nurse to pass messages related to the Jacobite plot (cf.** **ODNB** **). He was ultimately acquitted of the treason charges.** **4** **It is unclear whether Edwards is referring to a publication in this entry.**

Pierpont, Jr. (1699–1776), was Edwards’ fellow tutor at Yale and later brother-in-law. [203.†] Cardinal Petrucci Xtian Perfection Probably Pietro Matteo Petrucci (1636–1701), **Christian perfection, consisting in the love of God: explain’d in several letters to a lady, &c. Written originally in Italian by Cardinal Petrucci. Now render’d into English, with an account of the author**. . . (London, 1704). Along with Miguel de Molinos, Cardinal Petrucci, bishop of Jesi, Italy, was a Quietist, or one whose spiritual system centered on the complete annihilation of the human will before God. Quietism was condemned by Pope Innocent XI in 1687. In 1691 Petrucci resigned the government of his diocese after his own writings were condemned by the Inquisition. Quietism also influenced François de Salignac de la Mothe Fénelon (see nos. 462, 477, and 478). The unsigned preface to the English edition of Petrucci’s book noted that “Presbyterians” would find in it “the Points of Justification and Faith exactly conformable to their System” (p. A3).

A compilation of various authors,** **The Ladies Library** **was the most widely circulated women’s conduct book in the first half of the eighteenth century. Traditionally attributed to Sir Richard Steele (1672–1729), it is now known to have been compiled by the philosopher George Berkeley (1685–1753).** **1** **Edwards lent** **The Ladies Library** **more frequently than any other book listed in his “Account Book.” He apparently owned the third edition (London, 1722); see** **Works, 6,** **193–94** **n** **6.**

Originally published weekly and edited by John Trenchard (1669–1723) and Thomas Gordon (1691?–1750); first issued in one volume in 1721. Trenchard, an Anglican of deist inclination who often wrote under the pseudonym “Cato,” collaborated with Gordon, a Scottish-born pamphleteer, and one other author (possibly the deist Anthony Collins) in this oft-reprinted periodical against the alleged pretentions and false doctrines of the high-church clergy (cf. **ODNB**).

Written in Latine by Hugo Grotius; and now translated into English, with the addition of a seventh book, by Symon Patrick** **(London, 1680), DC (Latin edition). Patrick’s addition is identified in later editions as “a seventh book against the present Roman church.” Grotius (Huig de Groot) was a Dutch jurist famous for his contributions to international law as well as for his sympathies with the Remonstrants (Arminians). **of the world**(London, 1665– ). The longest-running scientific journal in the world, this semiannual publication of the Royal Society of London continues today as two journals, one dedicated to the biological sciences and the other to the physical sciences. Through the good graces of Massachusetts Superior Court Judge Paul Dudley, a member of the Royal Society, Edwards had apparently hoped to have his “Spider Letter” of October 31, 1723, published in **Philosophical Transactions.**The manuscript was never printed, perhaps because the journal had published three papers on spiders by English naturalist Martin Lister between 1669 and 1684 (see **Works, 6,**152–53, 163–69).

[266.†] the Chaldee Paraphrast That is, the Targums, the ancient Aramaic paraphrases of the Hebrew Bible. (“Chaldee” is an obsolete and misleading term for Aramaic.) Various editions existed, including a Latin translation published in the famous Antwerp Polyglot (8 vols., 1569–72) by printer Christopher Plantin (1520?–89). English editions of portions of the Targums included Henry Ainsworth (1571–1622?), **Annotations upon the five bookes of Moses, and the booke of the Psalms. Wherein the Hebrew words and sentences are compared with, and explained by the ancient Greeke and Chaldee versions**..., 2 vols. (London, 1622), DC, which Edwards cites in the “Blank Bible” (**Works, 24,**273); and John Gill (1697–1771), **An exposition of the Book of Solomon’s Song, commonly called Canticles. . . . To which is added, The Targum, or Chaldee paraphrase upon the whole book, faithfully translated out of the original Chaldee; together with some explanatory notes upon it**(London, 1728). Portions of the Old Testament were originally written in Aramaic, and Edwards noted these (under the heading “Parts of the Old Testament are written in Chaldee”) in his 1609 polyglot Bible (see nos. 1 and 265 above).

**ten for the instruction of a young nobleman**(London, 1704), followed by a second part, **A gentleman instructed in the true principles of religion, with a full confutation of atheism and latitudinarianism**(London, 1707), and a third part, **The gentleman instructed, in the way of conversation, entertainment of friends, management of his estate, company-keeping, traveling, &c. . . .**(London, no later than 1713). This anonymous work, which reached a tenth edition by 1731, was the product of William Darrell (1651–1721), an English-born Jesuit who taught in France. [302.†] The septuagint That is, the ancient Greek version of Hebrew Scripture, traditionally attributed to a group of seventy-two translators commissioned by Ptolemy Philadelphus (285–246 b.c.e.). A number of complete and partial editions had appeared in Europe by Edwards’ time, including those of David Mill (1692–1756), **Vetus Testamentum ex versione septuaginta**..., 2 vols. (Amsterdam, 1725); and Johannes Ernst Grabe (1666–1711), **Septuaginta interpretum**..., 6 vols. (Oxford, 1707–1709), DC (vol. 1). The ancient Jewish pseudepigraphic “Letter of Aristeas” detailing the legend of the Septuagint’s creation appeared in an English translation by Thomas Lewis (1689–1749?), **The history of the seventy two interpreters: . . . with all the circumstances of that illustrious transaction**(London, 1715).

The anonymous, privately printed first edition was followed by a second (1724), third (1725), and other signed editions. Benjamin Franklin, during his brief stint working for two London printers, helped compose the third edition (which he later erroneously identified as the second). William Diodate (d. 1751), an English-born immigrant to New Haven, Connecticut, was the town’s earliest known settler of Italian ancestry. He was a descendant of the Genevan Calvinist divine Giovanni Diodati (1576–1649), a participant in the Synod of Dort, whose** **Pious annotations upon the Holy Bible** **(English ed., London, 1643) Diodate donated to the infant Yale College in Saybrook in 1715.** **8**

Philip Gibbs (1696– 1752), a Presbyterian minister and author of a history of shorthand, sparked considerable controversy when he revealed his Unitarian leanings in **A letter to the congregation of Protestant dissenters at Hackney, amongst whom the author now ministers.**. . . (London, 1737); cf. **ODNB.**On Guyse, see no. 378. Published responses to Gibbs included an anonymous work, **The doctrines of the Gospel vindicated: in a second letter to Mr. Philip Gibbs**. . . (London, 1738). The letter from Benjamin Colman (1673–1747) to Edwards is not known to be extant. Edwards responded to Colman in a letter of May 27, 1738: “What you inform of Mr. Gibbs of Hackney looks very sorrowful, as many other things do respecting the present state of religion in England, which would be enough to sink the friends of Zion, were it not that God is wont often to appear wonderfully for her, at such times as when enemies have almost swallowed her up” (**Works, 16,**78).

Boston was a minister of the Church of Scotland; his** **Fourfold State,** **originally published anonymously, was the most frequently reprinted Scottish book of the eighteenth century, according to** **ODNB.** **The Scottish minister Thomas Gillespie, in a letter to Edwards of November 24, 1746, asked: “Are the works of the great Mr. Boston known in your country,viz. the Fourfold State of Man, View of the Covenant of Grace, and a Discourse on Afflictions, and Church communion, etc.** **3** **If not, inform me by your letter” (** **Works, 2,** **477). Edwards responded in a letter of September 4, 1747: “As to Mr. Boston’s view of the covenant of grace, I have had some opportunity with it, and I confess I did not understand his scheme delivered in that book. I have read his Fourfold State of Man, and liked it exceeding well. I think he therein shows himself to be a truly great divine” (** **Works, 2,** **489; cf.** **16,** **235). Flavius Josephus (c. 37–c. 100), Jewish historian, **De bello Judaico.**A notable English translation by Sir Roger L’Estrange (1616–1704) first appeared as **The wars of the Jews: in two books; with the most deplorable history of the siege and destruction of the city of Jerusalem . . .**(London, 1703). The Dummer Collection included this work as part of **The works of Flavius Josephus,**translated by Roger L’Estrange, 2nd ed., 3 vols. (London, 1709), a set given to Yale by colonial governor Sir Edmund Andros. A Boston imprint of **The wars of the Jews,**reprinted from the fourth London edition, appeared in 1719 (Evans 39706). Edwards’ other reference is to Joseph ben Gorion (9th or 10th century?), the pseudonymous author of **History of the Jews,**a work also known as the **Josippon**(for “Joseph”), first published in Hebrew in Mantua in 1474–76. A popular English condensation of this work, translated by Peter Morwen (d. 1573?), first appeared as **A compendious and most marueilous history of the latter tymes of the Iewes commune weale . . .**(London, 1558), with many editions thereafter, including Boston, 1718 (Evans 39767; actual publication not until 1722). The Dummer Collection included a complete Latin translation of the **Josippon**by Jean Gagnier (Oxford, 1706).

**[453.†] Osiander’s Abridgement of the Magdeburgensian Centuriatours. The “Centuriators of Magdeburg,” led by the Lutheran Matthias Flacius (1520–1575), were the authors of a multivolume history of the church. Though historians dispute whether Flacius was actually one of the authors, the project was driven by his conservative Gnesio-Lutheranism, which was strongly anti-Romanist and opposed to the conciliatory tendency of the Philippists, led by Philipp Melanchthon (1497–1560). The Centuriators, who derived their name from the “centuries” they used to periodize church history, “more or less invented the century as a significant unit of historical measurement.”** **5** **Cotton Mather advised: “I would have you, if you don’t wholly Peruse, yet by all means Possess, and often Visit, the Ecclesiastical History of the Magdebur**

Published for the sake of doing justice to the purchasers of the two first editions of that work**(London, 1751); cf. **ODNB. Clarissa,**an epistolary novel, tells the tragic story of the attempted seduction of a virtuous young woman, Clarissa Harlowe, by the rakish Robert Lovelace, who ultimately drugs and rapes her, plunging her temporarily into insanity before she dies in an attitude of both defiance and Christian resignation. **The Scots Magazine,**issued monthly in Edinburgh, January 1739 to December 1793. **The New-York Gazette,**issued weekly in New York, January 1747 to March 1759, and preceded and followed by similarly titled newspapers.

[574.] [§ no. 468] dr. doddridge in his appendix to vol. 3. p. 63. speaking of several Propositions tending to prove the Inspiration of the Old Testament has these words “But tis Obvious that the Illustration of all these Propositions would be the work of a large volume rather than of such a Postscript to a dissertation itself of so moderate a length. I have discussed them all with the most material objections which have been advanced against Them in that Course [*] of theological Lectures which I mentioned in the Preface to the first volume and which it is my continual Care to render worthy the Acceptance of the pub-lick in due Time by such Alterations & Additions as frequent Reviews in Conjunction with what occurs to me in reading conversation or meditation may suggest.” Philip Doddridge (1702–51), **Family Expositor**(see no. 290), Appendix 2, “Postscript.” Doddridge’s arguments for the divine inspiration of the Old Testament include the independent attestation of its “material Facts” in the “Heathen Writers,” as well as the fulfillment of its prophetic predictions. He also notes that “the facts asserted were of such a Nature, as could not possibly have gained Credit, had they been false” (pp. 61–63). Doddridge refers here to his **Course of lectures**(see no. 468).

**[593.†] Pamela or vertue Rewarded in 4 vol** **s** **in octavo. cum Privilegio <[§ no. 624]> Samuel Richardson (1689–1761),** **Pamela; or, Virtue rewarded. In a**

#### [Page 26, column 2]

**series of familiar letters from a beautiful young damsel to her parents: and afterwards, in her exalted condition, between her, and persons of figure and quality, upon the most important and entertaining subjects, in genteel life. . . . Publish’d in order to cultivate the principles of virtue and religion in the minds of the youth of both sexes,** **4 vols. (London, 1740– 41), AB. This immensely popular epistolary novel first appeared anonymously in two volumes in 1740. In response to numerous criticisms and parodies by Henry Fielding (1707–54), Eliza Hay-wood (1693?–1756), and others, Richardson published a two-volume sequel in 1741. The entire four-volume novel appeared in a deluxe, illustrated edition in 1742.** **4** **Edwards owned this or a later edition. The novel tells the story of Pamela Andrews, a servant girl, who is doggedly pursued by Mr. B., the son of her late mistress, who temporarily confines her in his country estate under the watchful eye of the cruel Mrs. Jewkes. Mr. B. eventually repents of his behavior and he and Pamela are reconciled and married. Though in the final two volumes Mr. B. has an affair with another woman, Pamela’s enduring patience and virtue lead him again to repent and pledge his unwavering fidelity.**

**[610.#] Amelia . a novel By HenryFielding Esq. 4. vol** **s** **. 12** **mo** **. much commended in monthly Review for decem. 1751 as recommending vertue and Conjugal Love. Henry Fielding (1707–54),** **Amelia,** **4 vols. (London, 1752).** **MR** **5 (1751). Fielding’s final novel is the story of Amelia Booth (partly modeled after Fielding’s first wife, Charlotte Cradock [d. 1744]), who patiently and lovingly endures the travails of married life with the penniless Captain Billy Booth, who is for a time thrown into prison because he cannot bribe a judge to gain his freedom. Eventually the parson, Dr. Harrison, helps Booth pay off his debts, and Booth returns to a happy life with Amelia, who inherits her mother’s fortune. Because of the novel’s indictment of prison conditions and laws pertaining to the poor,** **ODNB** **judges it “the first novel of social protest and reform in English.”**

[612.#] To Enquire after some Philosophical Treatise of the nature of Electricity the best that is extant. Various possibilities. Edwards probably made this entry soon after the celebrated publication of Benjamin Franklin (1706–90), **Experiments and observations on electricity, made in Philadelphia in America**(London, 1751, with a French translation published in Paris in 1752). Other possible texts include Benjamin Martin (1705– 82), **An essay on electricity: being an enquiry into the nature, cause and properties thereof, on the principles of Sir Isaac Newton’s theory of vibrating motion, light and fire . . .**(Bath, 1746); and Benjamin Wilson (1721–88), **A treatise on electricity**(London, 1750). Electricity was also treated in the earlier work of Francis Hauksbee (1660?– 1713), **Physico-mechanical experiments**(see no. 295). Two years after Edwards’ death, the founder of Methodism, John Wesley (1703–91), published anonymously **The desideratum; or, Electricity made plain and useful**(London, 1760), a treatise on electrotherapy.

[614.#] <The Book entitled> dialogues on Education Vol. 2. p. 21. menti speaking of the Books which Ey Euphranor, the Head of his Academy recommends for the forming just Principles concerning Government has these words “But above all the Immortal Harrington the great oracle of modern Politicks who by a fair and Full Induction of historical Facts has deduced the general Laws which introduce and govern the grand Crises and Revolutions of the political World and who upon these has erected a well balanced & incorruptible scheme of Government by which every other Form is to be estimated in and counted more or less perfect as it approaches to or recedes from it.” <[§ no. 640]> David Fordyce (1711–51), **Dialogues concerning education**(see no. 598). James Harrington (1611–77), **The commonwealth of Oceana**(see no. 566). Harrington’s celebrated work, first published in 1656 and dedicated to Oliver Cromwell, was hailed by the philosopher David Hume (1711–76) as the “only valuable model of a commonwealth” yet proposed (cf. **DNB**). Influenced by Machiavelli, Harrington proposed an elaborate system of checks and balances in government and a limit on the value of landed estates. After the Restoration, he was imprisoned for a time in the Tower of London.

[660.] [§ no. 571] In the Boston Evening Post <April 1. 1754> something being occasionally cited out of dr. Jacksons works Vol. I. He is spoken of said spoken of there as one of the greatest divines that ever England produced and Th his works as being publish’d an hundred years ago. **The Boston Evening-Post,**published weekly, 1735–75. An anonymous letter, printed on the front page of April 1, 1754, praises Thomas Jackson (1578–1640), dean of Peterborough, and quotes his **Works**(see no. 571), 1673 edition, p. 130, on the alleged danger of granting safe harbor to Jews: “So prodigious is all Appearance of Prosperity in those whom God has cursed, that when the Jews have Hopes of Ease and Welfare, it is an infallible Symptom of great Distemper in the publick State wherein they live.” The newspaper article goes on to reiterate medieval charges of Jewish river-poisoning, cannibalism, and the like. The article concludes: “Wolves and Bears will become mild as Domestick Creatures, by being housed and fed: The Jews alone, of all Animals, when harboured and well treated, grow more venomous and cruel.”

**T** **he list below presents the identifiable book entries, in alphabetical order, from Edwards’ “Account Book,” excluding references to his own published works. Whereas the “Catalogue” entries are presented in this volume as they appear in the manuscript, with annotations underneath, the “Account Book” entries are presented in alphabetical order, to avoid repetitive annotation of frequently lent titles. Thus, the annotated book references are presented by author or title (in boldface), followed by Edwards’ own verbatim notation(s). Book citations also appearing in the “Catalogue” are preceded by an asterisk (*) and followed by the entry number in which the title first appears (e.g., “C–198”). In cases where Edwards lent more than one book at a time to the same person, the full entry is given under each book reference. The manuscript page number on which each entry appears in the “Account Book” is given in brackets. Where Edwards does not supply the date, an approximate date, based on surrounding entries, is provided in brackets. Edwards’ own dates are in Old Style. Thus, a date between January 1 and March 24, 1734, is referred to as “1733/4” or “1733,4.” (Old Style notation ended in 1752 when Britain and its colonies finally followed the rest of Europe in adopting the Gregorian calendar.) Where approximate dates are provided in brackets, the year is given in New Style. Individuals referred to in the “Account Book” are identified in Appendix B, “Register of Persons to Whom Edwards Lent Books.”**

**and others, Richardson published a two-volume sequel in 1741. The entire four-volume novel appeared in a deluxe, illustrated edition in 1742.** **8** **Edwards owned this or a later edition. The novel tells the story of Pamela Andrews, a servant girl, who is doggedly pursued by Mr. B., the son of her late mistress, who temporarily confines her in his country estate under the watchful eye of the cruel Mrs. Jewkes. Mr. B. eventually repents of his behavior and he and Pamela are reconciled and married. Though in the final two volumes Mr. B. has an affair with another woman, Pamela’s enduring patience and virtue lead him again to repent and pledge his unwavering fidelity.**

Sherlock was bishop successively of Bangor, Salisbury (Sarum), and London. He wrote his **Letter,**which denounced the “Lewdness and Debauchery” of the common people in London and Westminster, after two small earthquakes struck the region on March 2, 1750 (cf. **ODNB**). Edwards received his copy of the **Letter**from Scottish correspondent John Erskine, to whom he wrote (November 15, 1750): “That these cities, and the nation, and indeed Christendom in general, are come to such a pass as they are, seems to me to argue that some very remarkable dispensation of divine providence is nigh, either of mercy or judgment; or perhaps both: of great mercy to an elect number, and great wrath and vengeance towards others” (**Works, 16,**364–65).

In this fifteen-page tract, Edwards’ grandfather Stoddard addressed ten miscellaneous questions, including: “Is it Lawfull [for men] to wear long Hair?” (No, he reasoned, based on 1 Cor. 11:14); and “Did we any wrong to the Indians in buying their Land at a small price?” (No, he argued, since “had it continued in their hands, it would have been of little value. It is our dwelling on it, and our improvements, that have made it to be of Worth”); pp. 4, 13.

This was perhaps the most forceful statement by Stoddard of his policy of opening communion to the unregenerate. It provoked a point-by-point rebuttal by Increase Mather (1639–1723), **A dissertation, wherein the strange doctrine lately published in a sermon, the tendency of which, is, to encourage unsanctified persons (while such) to approach the holy table of the Lord, is examined and confuted.**...(Boston, 1708), Evans 1366. Edwards abandoned his grandfather’s open communion policy in 1748, thereby hastening his estrangement from his Northampton congregation.

**I** **n 1732, Edwards and the other members of the Hampshire Association of Ministers (Hampshire County, Massachusetts) agreed to form a library for their common use (see Editor’s Introduction). Though no complete record of the library’s holdings is known to exist, the minutes of the association’s meetings between 1731 and 1747 reveal thirteen of the book titles sought or acquired by the ministers. The annotated book references are presented below in alphabetical order by author or title (in boldface), followed by page number in the minutes where the reference occurs, the verbatim notation made by the appointed note-taker, and the meeting date (in brackets). Edwards’ “Catalogue” parallels are indicated with a “C–” plus the entry number.**

### appendix a. timothy edwards’ library and reading edited and annotated by kenneth p. minkema

**T** **his appendix contains lists of books owned, cited, lent, and borrowed by Jonathan’s father, Timothy Edwards, pastor of East Windsor, Connecticut. The first section (A) is the inventory Timothy made of his trunk and desk drawer around 1719. The second (B) is the list of books drawn up as part of the probate record of his estate in 1771, with some of the books enumerated merely by author or lots rather than individually described. Section C is a list of books in the Beinecke Rare Book and Manuscript Library, Yale University, that have Timothy’s signature at the front, indicating that they were once part of his library. The next section (D) gathers books cited and excerpted by Timothy in his various manuscript notebooks. Section E shows his book lending and borrowing practices. Section F shows books Timothy sought to buy.**

Timothy Edwards’ library and book use is significant in itself as an example of book collecting in colonial Connecticut. By the time of his death, Timothy had collected close to eight hundred books and pamphlets. But his library was also an important lifelong resource for his children, including of course Jonathan, and, as the “Catalogue” clearly demonstrates, Jonathan and his father often borrowed books from each other throughout their lives.

#### Memd: of Books & Papers &c in My Trunk

manuscripts or printed works, but the sheer number of Mather titles in Timothy’s hands suggests that, within the Edwards family at least, the Mathers were so much an assumed part of the religious discourse that they did not warrant citation.

Several features of Timothy’s library bear emphasizing. First, as mentioned in the Editor’s Introduction, Timothy focused on “practical divinity,” or works treating the nature of Christian living, particularly afflictions and trials and their accompanying temptations to despair. Timothy also possessed many texts for educating children, reflecting his extra-ministerial vocation as a tutor for local boys. Finally, fully 20 percent of the titles are by Increase and Cotton Mather, who were important influences on Timothy and, through him, on Jonathan. Curiously, aside from his “Catalogue,” Jonathan barely mentions the Mathers in his

**[A55.] [ . . . ] M** **r** **Willards Brief Reply to G: K. at y** **e** **S. W Corner of y** **e** **T. Samuel Willard (1640–1707), minister of Groton, Massachusetts, and president of Harvard College,** **A brief reply to Mr. George Kieth** **[** **sic** **]:** **in answer to a script of his, entituled, A refutation of a dangerous and hurtfull opinion, maintained by Mr. Samuel Willard, &c.** **(Boston, 1703), Evans 1150. George Keith (1638–1715) was first a minister of the Church of Scotland, then converted to Quakerism and toured New England in the 1680s, then became an Episcopal priest in 1700 and was a missionary in America, 1702–4. This was the penultimate salvo in a long exchange between the two on various issues.** **3** **Willard was replying to Keith’s** **A refutation of a dangerous & hurtful opinion maintained by Mr. Samuel Willard, an independent minister at Boston, & president at the commencement in Cambridge in New-England, July 1, 1702: Viz. That the fall of Adam, and all the sins of men, necessarily come to pass by virtue of God’s decree, and his determination both of the will of Adam, and of all other men, to sin** **(New York, 1702), Evans 1053. Keith in turn responded to Willard’s** **Brief Reply** **with** **An answer to Mr. Samuell Willard (one of the ministers at Boston in New-England): his reply to my printed sheet, called, A dangerous and hurtful opinion maintained by him, viz. That the fall of Adam, and all the sins of men necessarily come to pass by virtue of Gods decree, and his determining both of the will of Adam, and of all other men to sin** **(New York, 1704), Evans 1160.**

3. The first exchange, about a decade previous, was ecclesiological. Keith began with **The Presbyterian and independent visible churches in New-England and else-where, brought to the test, and examined according to the doctrine of the Holy Scriptures, in their doctrine, ministry, worship, constitution, government, sacraments and Sabbath Day, and found to be no true church of Christ. More particularly directed to these in New-England, and more generally to those in old-England, Scotland, Ireland, &c. With a call and warning from the Lord to the people of Boston and New-England, to repent, &c. And two letters to the preachers in Boston; and an answer to the gross abuses, lyes and slanders of Increas**[sic] **Mather**

<!-- p. 261 -->

**and Samuel Norton, &c.**(Philadelphia, 1689), Evans 472. Willard, Cotton Mather, and others responded with **The principles of the Protestant religion maintained: and churches of New-England, in the profession and exercise thereof defended, against all the calumnies of one George Keith, a Quaker, in a book lately published at Pensilvania**[**sic**], **to undermine them both**(Boston, 1690), Evans 502.

The manuscripts of Timothy’s ordination sermon (he had settled in East Windsor in 1694 but was ordained May 28, 1698), as well as his “Thick paper Book,” are lost. (The latter may have been his vindication of Solomon Stoddard’s **Doctrine of Instituted Churches**[see list of lent books, no. E12]). While at Harvard College from 1686 to 1688, Timothy attended the Boston First Church, where he heard and made the acquaintance of Increase and Cotton Mather, and made notes of their sermons. The Mathers’ significant influence on Edwards is reflected in this catalogue.

[B2.] 4 volumes of neals History of the puritans Daniel Neal (1678–1743), **The history of the Puritans; or, Protestant Non-conformists, from the Reformation to the death of Queen Elizabeth, with an account of their principles, their attempts for a further reformation in the church, their sufferings, and the lives and characters of their principal divines,**4 vols. (London, 1732).

1. Inventoried by Ebenezer Grant and David Bissell of East Windsor; Bissell apparently wrote all but the final few items of the entire inventory. Two people typically worked together in making estate inventories of book collections; one would read off the book’s “binder’s title” on the spine (the title supplied by the binder, not necessarily matching the book’s actual title) and the other person would write down what he heard. Not surprisingly, this method was not foolproof and produced ambiguities for later readers (see, e.g. B78, “Day and Rhetorick,” below).

## appendix b. register of persons to whom edwards lent books

**T** **he individuals identified below are listed in Edwards’ “Account Book” (Beinecke Rare Book and Manuscript Library, Yale University, Gen. MSS 151, Box 21, f. 1267). The entries here are listed by the name of the lendee, with the specific books lent, the page number in the “Account Book,” and the date. Books lent to each person are listed in chronological order of transaction. Unless otherwise indicated, towns are in Massachusetts. Information on Northampton inhabitants is from James Russell Trumbull, “History of Northampton: Northampton Genealogies, V. 3, Pt. 1,” typescript, Forbes Library, Northampton, Massachusetts.**

**T** **his list of printed works includes items that Edwards directly cited or from which he quoted. It excludes titles that were part of excerpts or cited at secondhand. In each citation, bibliographical details (including publication date) are listed as they appear in earlier volumes of** **The Works of Jonathan Edwards** **(1957–2007). Volume and page numbers are given, as well as references in Edwards’ unpublished manuscripts.
